According to recent reports, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, if I’ve learned anything over the past few years, it’s to just say yes. Saying the word was simple, but ended up changing my relationship with fitness—and transforming my whole life.

Industry observers note that I’ve always loved being physically active and moving my body; I ran track and field in high school, played field hockey in both high school and college, and enjoyed horseback riding as a young adult. But shortly after graduating, I had my first of seven children at 23. From that point on, I went straight into parenting mode: My family became my priority, and with so much to juggle, exercise took a back seat for the next few decades.

But at 55, I wanted to feel strong in my body again. My kids were grown and I had more free time, so I signed up for a gym membership. I even started working with a personal trainer to make sure I was doing the right moves safely. Over the next 15 years, I exercised with several trainers, lifting light weights once or twice a week with dumbbells and weight machines. I enjoyed the workouts and saw improvements to my overall fitness, but I wasn’t particularly passionate about going to the gym, so I wasn’t always consistent and never set any real goals.

Then, at 70, everything changed. My trainer who I had come to enjoy working with and trust moved away, and without that connection, I stopped going to the gym. But after about a year away, the fitness manager at my gym, Nate Fleming, reached out to me, and I began working with him twice a week.

He immediately changed up my programming and introduced me to the idea of progressive overload. I learned that gradually increasing the weight I lifted each week could help me build muscle, get stronger, and see real results. He also added new movements to my routine, like farmer’s carries, deadlifts, and squat variations. Deadlifts, in particular, became one of my favorite exercises—I loved that the move required so much technique. There was something so satisfying about picking up a heavy weight and realizing I could lift more than I thought.

Nearly overnight, my attitude toward fitness changed: I enjoyed being challenged and discovering how much stronger I could become when I pushed myself. Over the next year, I began to see visible muscle definition in my arms and legs and felt more energized throughout the day. More importantly, though, my confidence skyrocketed because I had developed a greater trust in my own abilities.

I had grown to love lifting heavy, and wanted to step outside my comfort zone and discover what I could accomplish in my 70s. I casually asked Nate if there were deadlifting competitions for older women, and he said there were. So, I took a leap of faith and started a seven-month training process for a powerlifting competition (which took place this past March). I upped my training to three days a week, continuing to progressively increase the weights, and worked on refining my technique to move more efficiently.

Sources indicate that the day of the competition was one of the best days of my life. I decided to compete in all three lifts: I squatted 132 pounds, bench-pressed 71.5 pounds, and deadlifted 242 pounds, setting records in all three lifts for my age and weight category in Nova Scotia, Canada, where I live. I was so proud of what I’d accomplished and felt incredibly empowered by what my body could do at 71. My kids and grandkids were also there to cheer me on, which made the day even more special. Sharing that moment with my family and showing them what was possible at my age meant so much to me. I walked away feeling stronger, more confident, and excited to do it again.

My next powerlifting competition is this month, and I still lift with Nate three days a week. My training is structured in four-week blocks, and the weight, sets, and reps change each week. For instance, in week one, I might do 3 sets of 5 reps at a moderate weight. Then, I gradually increase the load in weeks two and three while lowering the reps as I get closer to my heaviest lifts. Week four is a deload week, so I reduce the weight and give my body a chance to recover before lifting heavier again.

It has been revealed that each workout starts with the main lift (deadlift, squat, or bench press) because that’s when I have the most energy. Then, I move on to three or four accessory exercises, where I use lighter weights to strengthen supporting muscles, address weaknesses, and improve my performance in the main lifts. For example, on deadlift day, I might incorporate exercises like lunges, hamstring curls, and bent-over rows to strengthen my glutes, hamstrings, and back.

In a recent development, I’m incredibly proud of my progress over the last six months. I have a lingering shoulder injury, so right now, my bench press has stayed about the same at 71.5 pounds. But I can squat 160 pounds and deadlift 265 pounds, which is only five pounds away from the Canadian deadlift record.

Industry observers note that while I train hard, I recover even harder in between sessions. I get seven to eight hours of sleep each night and am mindful about nutrition, eating lots of protein, since it’s important for building and maintaining muscle. I aim for around 120 grams a day, with eggs, chicken, and fish as some of my go-to sources. Additionally, during rest days, I focus on stretching and hip and shoulder mobility to improve my range of motion. I don’t count my steps, but I try to walk as much as I can throughout the day to keep my body moving and maintain cardiovascular health.

Feetures Elite Ultra Light Quarter Sock.

I love Feetures socks for their snug arch support and gentle compression that keeps them comfortably in place during workouts.

Clif Builders are my favorite post-workout snack since they taste great and pack 20 g of protein per bar.

Sources indicate that when I first decided to work with a personal trainer in my 50s, I wanted guidance, accountability, and the confidence that I was exercising safely and effectively—and I got that. My first few trainers helped me build a foundation by teaching me proper form and the fundamental movements that I still rely on today.

But working with Nate completely changed my relationship with lifting: He knows how to motivate me, pushing me without going beyond my abilities. When I attempt a latest personal record, his belief in me helps me believe in myself, too. Now, I know what I’m capable of and how to challenge myself while lifting safely. The gym has become so much more than a place to work out—it’s where I keep discovering what I can do.

According to recent reports, I’ve learned that getting stronger isn’t just about how hard I work in the gym—it’s also about how well I recover between workouts through getting plenty of sleep, mobility work, stretching, and walking. When I don’t make time for recovery activities or I don’t fuel properly, it makes a difference; I feel more fatigued, have less energy during workouts, and struggle to perform at the same level.

For me, progress doesn’t mean pushing myself to the limit every day. It means finding the right balance between challenging my body and giving it the rest and support it needs to keep getting stronger.

If you’d told me a few years ago that I’d be powerlifting in my 70s and chasing a deadlift record, I never would have believed you. Before I started training with Nate, I had never really set significant fitness goals or thought about pushing my limits. But that began to change when I realized how much stronger I could become with the right coaching and encouragement. I was inspired to set goals that challenged me in new ways I never thought possible, and I’ve learned that it’s never too late to surprise myself and try something new. Having a goal to work toward keeps me motivated, and I love seeing how far I can push myself when I have the right support and proposal in place.

It has been revealed that of course, getting stronger takes patience, consistency, and a willingness to step outside my comfort zone, but the reward is so worth it. I hope my journey encourages other women, especially those in their 60s and 70s, to keep challenging themselves and try fresh things. They might discover a passion they never knew they had, just as I did.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that new EV prices edged up in October, but buyers still paid less than they did a year ago. The average transaction price for a new EV in the US was $56,220, up 1% from September and down 2.7% from October 2025, according to Kelley Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand.

Across all latest vehicles, the average hit a record $51,109, up 1.3% from September and 2.1% year over year, even as prices rose more slowly than they typically do in October.

Recent findings suggest that EV incentives barely budged from September’s revised 11.2% of the average transaction price to 11.3% in October. That’s up from 10.3% a year earlier and well above October’s industrywide average of 6.8%.

Tesla’s average selling price fell from September to $54,194, but it was still up 1.2% year over year. The Cybertruck helped push that average higher. Cox Automotive estimates Tesla sold 1,914 Cybertrucks in October, its best month in more than a year, at an average price of $92,380.

Recent findings suggest that the sad thing is that there likely is a market for an affordable electric pickup truck in the U.S. to compete with Ford’s F150 and others. The Ford Fathom may be the best fit for that market, now.

Sources indicate that that sales bump comes as Tesla prepares to end Cybertruck production at its Austin factory in mid-2027. Elon Musk mentioned Tesla will dismantle the assembly line around June or July to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis.

Mel Robbins has always been a mover—running, hiking, skiing, Pilates, yoga, you name it—but it’s only been recently that the 58-year-old has added strength training to her fitness regimen. She credits Dr. Stacy Sims (a Women’s Health advisory board member) and Dr. Vonda Wright, both guests on The Mel Robbins Podcast, with finally persuading her to lift weights.

Recent findings suggest that “They kept saying, when we reach a certain age, 40 and up, for us to start resistance training and with heavier weights,” says Mel, who had to overcome a few fitness myths to finally prioritize pumping iron. “I was nervous I would bulk up. That's a joke, because you know how much you need to train to actually bulk up? I wasn't going to be doing that.”.

So what exactly does Mel do in the gym? She walked WH through a typical session for the latest episode of Strong Like.

In a recent development, before Mel’s feet ever touch a mat, she makes sure to jot down—with actual pen and paper!—what she intends to do at the gym. “This will ensure that you actually do it, because if you're relying on this noggin up here, it ain't happening,” she claims.

Sources indicate that with her to-do list by her side, Mel begins her session with a warm-up. She runs through a batter of stretches that include inchworms (with an added push-up—go Mel!) and lunges with a twist, before moving on to a banded overhead press to mobilize her shoulders. “I've stopped judging these little bands,” Mel says. “These little suckers look like nothing. Let me tell you, there's a whole lot of something in these bands. You'll be shocked at how much gain you can get and how great this is for you.”.

In a recent development, with her warm-up complete, she moves on to the workout, shifting the bands from her arms to her legs for a duck walk. Mimicking the water fowl, she moves forward and back, side to side, keeping outward pressure on the bands.

Next, she tackles one of her favorite moves, a reverse lunge with medicine ball twist. “It's a compound movement that works mobility, your core, your arms, your legs, everything in one movement,” Mel says. “It's super-simple, painful, and awful, and it works like a charm.”.

Sources indicate that she moves on to the upper body with chest presses, though she has a hack for lighting up even more muscles in the process. “If you want to maximize what you're doing here, suck in your stomach and clench your butt, because then it's not just arms; it's a whole-body thing,” she indicates.

Finally, she concludes with a snatch, joking: “You can work out a lot of aggression at the world doing [these].”.

Sources indicate that ultimately, says Mel, her approach to fitness is pretty straightforward: “I'm not in here because I want to look good in a bathing suit. I do, but that's not the motivation. I'm in here lifting weights because I want to live a long, vibrant, healthy life. I want to be dancing into my late 90s. I want to make sure I can pick up the suitcase and put it up in the overhead. I want to make sure that I am strong so my life is long.”.

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1075 w)

Lucid CEO admits it ‘did not even know where cars were’ and lost orders

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the tech giant’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.
  • Recent findings suggest that that’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles.
  • According to recent reports, napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the tech giant’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles. And it’s a problem Tesla ran into, and fixed, back in 2018 at more than ten times Lucid’s current volume.

According to recent reports, napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter. He said that at the start of Q3, the manufacturer had orders where it “would take sometimes two weeks to deliver to the customer, and so we would lose the order.”.

In a recent development, he noted Lucid now has visibility on which cars are being built, where they’re shipped, where they’re stored, and when they can reach a customer. A new commercial team also now sells the cars it knows are available on the day a customer wants one.

According to recent reports, lucid built 3,228 more vehicles than it delivered in the first half of 2026, including 5,500 built but only 3,093 delivered in Q1. Its inventory hit $1.38 billion on the balance sheet at the end of June, which is why we reported earlier this year that Lucid had to adjust production after a bloated Q1 inventory.

So Lucid had thousands of cars on lots and in transit, and it was still losing buyers because it couldn’t match a car to an order fast enough.

In Q3, Lucid cut production to 2,954 vehicles and delivered 3,806, down 7% year over year. Finished goods inventory fell by almost 15% during the quarter, according to new CFO Alexander De Bock. Inventory stood at $1.22 billion on September 30.

Tesla learned this lesson the hard way during the Model 3 ramp.

By Q3 2018, Tesla was making roughly 4,000 Model 3s per week. That’s more cars every week than Lucid delivers in a full quarter today. Deliveries tripled or quadrupled in some markets, and the bottleneck moved from the factory to the trucks.

According to recent reports, elon Musk tweeted in September 2018 that Tesla had “gone from production hell to delivery logistics hell.” A week later, he remarked Tesla was facing an “extreme shortage of car carrier trailers” and had started building its own car carriers to keep cars moving. Tesla also launched door-to-door delivery and asked existing owners to help at delivery centers.

It didn’t stop there. In November 2018, with the federal tax credit about to be cut in half for Tesla buyers, Musk said Tesla had bought trucking companies and locked in contracts with major haulers. Tesla moved cars east by truck instead of rail to cut weeks off transit times.

Tesla delivered 83,500 vehicles in Q3 2018, including 55,840 Model 3s, a record at the time.

When Model 3 reached Europe in February 2019, the first ship docked at Zeebrugge in Belgium and Tesla immediately had trouble processing the cars at the port.

According to recent reports, about a week after the first ship arrived, Tesla ended its contract with the company preparing Model 3s at the port and took over the work itself. The target was 3,000 cars per week coming through one port.

It has been revealed that it worked. By March 2019, Tesla delivered more than 5,300 Model 3s in Norway alone, making it the best-selling car in the country by a wide margin. A car that’s sitting at a port or on a lot doesn’t make anyone money. Tesla treated delivery speed as a sales tool, not a back-office job.

We later learned from Musk himself that this “logistic hell” was almost the nail in Tesla’s coffin. The CEO said that Tesla was at the brink of bankruptcy at the time.

I like to think people were relatively patient with Tesla's growing pains when Model 3 was ramping up in 2018, largely because there weren't many alternatives for a sporty, relatively affordable EV.

In a recent development, but it's 2026. Buyers have plenty of options now, and the patience that early EV adopters once had for these kinds of mistakes is long gone.

According to recent reports, this is one of the most embarrassing admissions we’ve heard on an earnings call, and credit to Napoli for saying it out loud. Most executives would have blamed “demand” and moved on.

In a recent development, but it explains a lot. Lucid’s problem has never been the cars. The Air and Gravity are excellent products. The problem has been everything around them: service, software, and now we learn, basic inventory tracking. When you’re spending about $273,000 for every car you deliver, losing a buyer because you can’t find their car two weeks after they ordered is brutal.

Tesla solved this at 4,000 Model 3s a week while fighting for its own survival. Lucid is moving fewer than 300 cars a week. This isn’t a hard problem at that scale. It’s a discipline problem, and Napoli is right to call it that.

#5793. Industry News: Theaster Gates is Changing the Future of American Fine China

Industry News: Theaster Gates is Changing the Future of American Fine China

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It all started when Theaster Gates wanted to throw a dinner party.
  • It has been revealed that “My friends were like, ‘Oh, you should work with Pickard,’ ” Gates recalls, referring to the last remaining producer of porcelain tableware in the US, founded in 1893 and headquartered since 1930 in Antioch, Illinois.
  • “I came to the warehouse and realized that the manufacturer had had better days,” Gates says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It all started when Theaster Gates wanted to throw a dinner party. The Chicago-based artist, whose practice blends ceramics, painting, performance, and urban renewal, imagined inviting 200 guests on each of five nights. Central to the project, he envisioned creating all the tableware himself.

It has been revealed that “My friends were like, ‘Oh, you should work with Pickard,’ ” Gates recalls, referring to the last remaining producer of porcelain tableware in the US, founded in 1893 and headquartered since 1930 in Antioch, Illinois. When he told Pickard he would need some 10,000 items, the firm admitted such an order would be daunting but invited him to visit.

“I came to the warehouse and realized that the manufacturer had had better days,” Gates says. “I’m wanting to say this with a lot of dignity, but as we moved between tarps and equipment, it became clear that the company was just doing what it could to stay alive.”.

China dishware fills two rolling racks at the Pickard factory in Illinois, which was recently purchased by Theaster Gates.

Gates at the Pickard facility with molds for dishware.

Recent findings suggest that pickard’s august history of commissions includes White House services for first ladies Laura Bush and Michelle Obama, as well as the official State Department dinnerware used in US embassies around the world. Once an essential element of bridal registries, fine china has waned in popularity, however, along with the tradition of formal entertaining at home. After CEO Andy Pickard Morgan, a member of the fourth generation of the family to run the business, acknowledged that he was ready to call it a day, one thing led to another, and Gates says, “I am now the owner of Pickard China.”.

In a recent development, his acquisition might seem out of character. Gates has forged a formidable reputation for himself and his Rebuild Foundation by buying rundown buildings in Chicago’s historically Black South Side, then converting them into thriving arts and education hubs. An abandoned residence is now the Black Cinema House; a century-old savings and loan is now the Stony Island Arts Bank, which mounts exhibitions and safeguards historical collections. Pickard, meanwhile, is located in a quiet, predominantly white village on the Wisconsin border, some 67 miles from his studio on Chicago’s South Side.

A Pickard artisan finishing a plate.

Gates, funnel in hand, surrounded by artifacts of the Pickard process.

Pickard pieces line plywood racks.

But Gates does not see a contradiction. For starters, he indicates, his interest in craft transcends racial or ethnic origins; one formative experience was studying with master potters in Japan. Gates notes that while many of his collections relate to Black culture, he also took on the late scholar Robert Bird’s library of films by the Russian director Andrei Tarkovsky and the classical music archive of the LaSalle Quartet, whose core members were Jewish. “I have those because they are rich, and someone passed, and those things needed a latest life,” he explains. “The problem of the archive is not one of Black or white; it’s one of stewardship and imagination.” He has even shown an affinity for luxury goods, having made ceramic vessels for Prada Home in Milan this past April.

Pickard also presents the kind of major, multifaceted problem Gates, who holds a master’s degree in urban planning, says “makes me feel alive as an artist,” in this case encompassing craftsmanship and legacy, as well as the value of labor and community. His intends are still developing but include upgrading the facilities, rethinking the product line, and beefing up the staff, which now stands at 14 full-time employees, down from dozens at the firm’s height. Preserving their know-how for posterity is a priority. “I want this really capable team to train a newly introduced generation of descalers and liners and glazers,” he says. Also definite: The company will continue operating in the commercial sphere, and he will use its massive kilns to fire his own large sculptures, something he’s wanted to do for a decade. “I’m thinking about manufacturing ceramics as an extension of my practice,” he notes.

A Pickard artisan filling molds.

The Pickard logo emblazoned on a wall.

Gates has worked with a variety of materials over the years, including tar paper—a nod to his roofer father—and salvaged fire hoses, which reference Civil Rights Era marchers who were blasted with water by police. Ceramics, though, were the focus of his formal studies and remain at the heart of his practice. “When I was training, I touched porcelain, but I was always a rough stoneware guy,” he indicates. “The more grog and sand and feldspar, the better.”.

Today Gates considers porcelain “an amazing craft” and expects the workshop to become “a playground for artistic promise,” where he, together with staff and visiting artists alike, can “dream about a raw material that could be anything.”.

Setting the table with bone china may no longer be the signifier of position and civility it once was, but Gates believes there’s still room for appreciation, as both an instrument of ritual and a family heirloom. “Legacy objects play a huge role in how we remember our grandparents, our parents, and our past,” he says.

And Gates’s own party is very much still on the table, so to speak. “Porcelain things are beautiful objects, but I’m drawn as much to the use of the thing as I am to the thing,” he says. “The idea that I could make large works of art with porcelain is exciting, but I’m also excited to be able to host a thousand-person dinner and make all the wares for it.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that well, movement, it seems, has played an integral part.
  • But she’s also committed to consistent, everyday movement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that earlier this year, Susan Young Browne from Delaware celebrated her 108th birthday—the news of which travelled across the world. Everyone wanted to know the retired teacher’s longevity secrets. How did Susan, who had just renewed her driving license until 2033, retain such a good quality of life?

Sources indicate that well, movement, it seems, has played an integral part. Firstly, Susan, who still walks unassisted, told TODAY that she continues to attend chair dancing classes at a local community centre.

But she’s also committed to consistent, everyday movement.

Susan begins every morning with a 10-minute stretching, strengthening, and balancing routine.

With flexibility, mobility, strength and balance all being key markers of longevity, Susan’s routine is a reminder that workouts do not need to be long and complicated to have far-reaching benefits.

Another key part of Susan’s daily exercise routine that likely contributes to her impressive healthspan (the number of years spent living in good health and free from chronic disease)? Her focus on leg strength.

It has been revealed that “I get up and stand against the wall and exercise my legs. I make sure my legs are exercised,” Susan told TODAY.

Not only do strong legs help us move freely and reduce fall risk, but a growing body of evidence also points to an association between lower-body strength and cognitive function—another key element of longevity.

Sources indicate that one oft-cited study found that older adults with greater leg strength had 34% lower odds of low cognitive function than those with weaker legs. Meanwhile, a 10-year study of more than 300 twin sisters reported “a striking protective relationship” between leg power and cognition. The twin with greater leg power at the beginning of the study maintained their cognitive function better and indicated fewer age-related brain changes over the following decade.

While the exact mechanisms behind this association remain unclear, among scientists’ hypotheses are that stronger muscles may improve blood flow to the brain, that resistance training may influence nervous system function, and that lower-body strength can help preserve walking speed and mobility—both of which have been associated with a lower risk of dementia.

Using a wall for support, Susan can be seen balancing on one leg, which is a simple, effective, single-leg exercise that supports strength and balance.

It has been revealed that another simple move that only requires a wall? As the name suggests, a wall sit.

“Defined as an isometric exercise—an exercise where the working muscle doesn’t change length during the exercise and the joint doesn’t move—wall sits are super safe to perform, and put very little stress on the spine,” personal trainer Aimee Victoria Long previously explained to Women’s Health.

Mainly targeting the quadriceps (the muscles at the front of your thigh that support knee stability and everyday functional movements such as walking, getting up from a chair, and climbing stairs), wall sits can also improve endurance, balance, core, and lower-back strength.

It has been revealed that another simple, no-equipment exercise that supports functional lower-body strength is the humble bodyweight squat. Plus, one study even found that doing 60 seconds of squatting exercises during long periods of sitting may help preserve cognitive function.

Kia releases two latest PV5 electric van variants in the UK

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kia opened orders for two latest PV5 electric van variants, the PV5 Chassis and PV5 Cargo L2/H2, in the UK.
  • Industry observers note that the PV5 is Kia’s first fully electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) business.
  • So far, the PV5 has mostly been available in Passenger and Cargo body styles with several different variations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kia opened orders for two latest PV5 electric van variants, the PV5 Chassis and PV5 Cargo L2/H2, in the UK.

Industry observers note that the PV5 is Kia’s first fully electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) business. Built on Hyundai Motor’s dedicated modular skateboard platform, E-GMP.S, Kia can easily swap body styles to enable “limitless possibilities.”.

So far, the PV5 has mostly been available in Passenger and Cargo body styles with several different variations.

Sources indicate that kia added the PV5 Chassis, an open-bed model that can be converted into just about anything. In the UK, Kia is offering conversions through TGS Automotive Group, including lightweight tipper, Dropside, and Box solutions.

The PV5 Chassis is available exclusively with the long-range 71.2 kWh battery in the UK, which Kia mentioned could offer a potential WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km).

For reference, the PV5 Cargo L2/H1, which uses the same 71.2 kWh battery, offers a WLTP range of up to 258 miles (416 km). Other markets will also have a standard-range 51.1 kWh option.

The Chassis model is 4,610 mm long, 1,895 mm wide, and 1,935 mm tall, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.

Its compact size and 5.5-meter turning radius, Kia remarked, make it easy to maneuver in city streets, construction sites, and other tight work areas.

Inside, the PV5 Chassis features two seats. Like other variants, it includes a 12.9″ navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

Recent findings suggest that the Chassis model supports DC fast charging up to 120 kW, enabling the battery to charge from 10% to 80% in about 30 minutes. Using an 11 kW AC supply, it takes about 6 hours and 30 minutes to charge from 10% to 100%.

It has been revealed that payload depends on the configuration. Kia noted the Dropside offers a payload of up to 633 kg, while the Tipper can carry 561 kg.

In the UK, the PV5 Chassis is now on sale from £32,916 ($43,400) on the road, including the expected £5,000 ($6,700) UK Zero Emission Van Grant.

Sources indicate that however, it’s an “incomplete vehicle,” as Kia describes it. The converted PV5 Dropside is priced from £40,110 ($53,500) on the road, including the ZEVG, while the PV5 Tipper starts at £41,310 ($55,000).

Kia also rolled out the larger PV5 Cargo L2/H2 in the UK. The fresh variant is 4,695mm long, 1,895mm wide, and 2,200mm high, with a 2,995mm wheelbase.

The taller roof opens up an internal cargo-area height of 1,815mm. It also offers a greater load capacity than the L1/H1 and L2/H2, with 5.2 cubic meters.

Sources indicate that it’s available in three- and four-door configurations with the choice of two or three seats. The three-door versions have a maximum payload of 630 kg, while the four-door models have dual sliding doors and offer a payload of up to 600 kg. Both versions can tow up to 1,500 kg.

Like the Chassis model, the PV5 Cargo L2/H2 is available in the UK exclusively with the 71.2 kWh battery, which provides a WLTP range of up to 239 miles.

Inside, it features the same setup as the other PV5 variants, including a 12.9″ touchscreen navigation screen and a 7.5″ driver display.

The base PV5 Cargo L2/H2 Essential two-seat starts at £35,016 ($46,700), on the road, including ZEVG.

Bitcoin Price Slumps Under $62,000, Crashing 25% in One Month

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (624 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The bitcoin price slumped under $62,000 on Thursday afternoon, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, extending a slide of about 24% in one month as Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut set off a broad selloff in tech stocks.
  • In a recent development, bitcoin was trading near $81,800 on Oct.
  • Recent findings suggest that the slide came in steps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bitcoin price slumped under $62,000 on Thursday afternoon, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, extending a slide of about 24% in one month as Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut set off a broad selloff in tech stocks.

In a recent development, bitcoin was trading near $81,800 on Oct. 19. It touched a low of about $61,650 on Thursday, its weakest level since July, before steadying near $62,200. The drop was about 25% from the Oct. 19 close, based on daily data.

Recent findings suggest that the slide came in steps. Bitcoin closed near $80,050 on Oct. 25, about $78,250 on Nov. 1 and about $74,750 on Nov. 8. The steepest leg came last week, when it fell about 12.6% to a Nov. 15 close near $65,300, and the losses have continued this week.

Bitcoin had climbed back to about $64,000 early Thursday as Anthropic’s record IPO lifted stock futures, as this morning’s report revealed. The rally faded once U.S. markets opened. The bitcoin price fell from roughly $63,900 at the opening bell to about $62,200 by midday.

Anthropic shares opened shortly before noon at $111.50, 34% above the $83 IPO price, CNBC reported. The opening trade valued the Claude maker at more than $2 trillion. The stock quickly pulled back and was last near $97, about 17% above its offering price.

According to recent reports, the broader market went the other way. The major averages fell to session lows soon after Anthropic began trading, as investors took profits on the AI trade. The Nasdaq Composite dropped about 2% after gaining as much as 2% earlier in the session, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost about 1,000 points.

Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, told CNBC the premarket rally had faded even before Anthropic began trading. He called it the latest round of “sell the rally” trading. Nvidia (NVDA) fell about 3%, and the S&P 500 headed toward a sixth straight loss, the AP reported.

According to recent reports, the Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street’s fear gauge, climbed to about 28 after touching nearly 29 shortly after Anthropic began trading. That was its highest level since March, up from about 24.6 at Wednesday’s close. The bitcoin price moved in step with the Nasdaq through the afternoon.

Recent findings suggest that crypto stocks followed the Nasdaq lower in late-afternoon trading, about 3:55 p.m. ET. Strategy (MSTR) traded near $86.70, down about 4% on the day. Galaxy Digital (GLXY) dropped about 6.9%, the steepest decline in the group.

Coinbase (COIN) slipped about 0.9% to near $109.50, while Circle (CRCL) fell about 2.2%. Bitcoin miners gave back their early rally too. IREN (IREN) fell about 5.6%, CleanSpark (CLSK) lost about 5.4% and MARA Holdings (MARA) declined about 4.2%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) was down about 2.9%.

The Fed remains a headwind. Bets on a December rate hike have grown after minutes from the October meeting showed more policymakers backing higher rates, and some officials called for a half-point move.

The bitcoin price is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be its second-longest losing streak after nine weeks of declines in 2022. The streak has erased roughly $20,000 from the bitcoin price since mid-October, based on daily closes. Bitcoin price hit its weakest level since July on Thursday, and the Fed meets again next month.

Industry observers note that longer-term holders have not left. Institutional investors added 49,229 BTC through U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs in the third quarter, lifting their holdings to a record 356,491 BTC. Swiss bank Sygnum called the current downturn the shallowest bear market to date and sees a path to a fresh high near $128,000.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,900.

#5783. Tesla tuner Unplugged offers to take over Cybertruck production

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1180 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla tuner Unplugged offers to take over Cybertruck production

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unplugged Performance, the biggest name in Tesla aftermarket tuning, wants to keep the Cybertruck alive.
  • It comes just four days after Elon Musk noted Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027, with the truck selling at roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year Tesla planned for.
  • UP posted the pitch on X as “an open offer to Tesla.” The company says it fully supports putting Cybercab first and would run Cybertruck production “at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unplugged Performance, the biggest name in Tesla aftermarket tuning, wants to keep the Cybertruck alive. The firm publicly offered on Tuesday to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands, funded by a consortium of investors.

It comes just four days after Elon Musk noted Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027, with the truck selling at roughly 12% of the 250,000 units a year Tesla planned for.

UP posted the pitch on X as “an open offer to Tesla.” The company says it fully supports putting Cybercab first and would run Cybertruck production “at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus.”.

According to recent reports, in exchange, Tesla would collect a license fee plus FSD and Robotaxi network revenue on every vehicle built. UP even offered to let Cybercab get first call on battery cells. “We’ll wait our turn,” the manufacturer wrote.

UP founder Ben Schaffer made it clear that he supports Tesla’s all-in move to autonomy, but he wants to keep the Cybertruck program alive.

And it isn’t stopping at the pickup. UP states it would build the Cybertruck, a three-row “CyberSUV,” and an unmanned “CyberCargo” hauler. Two vehicles Tesla has sometimes referenced, but they were never unveiled.

Industry observers note that the post passed 240,000 views within hours, and the replies are mostly Cybertruck owners and Tesla shareholders begging Musk to say yes. Neither Musk nor Tesla had publicly responded at the time of writing.

Recent findings suggest that UP has a lot riding on this. It sells an entire Cybertruck product line, the UP Invincible lift and armor kits, and it has scored several contracts to turn Cybertrucks into police vehicles for law enforcement agencies. CEO Ben Schaffer once described the manufacturer’s purpose as doing “the things that Tesla maybe wants to do, but doesn’t have the bandwidth to do.” This is that idea taken to its extreme.

According to recent reports, musk framed the Cybertruck’s end as a space problem. He stated Tesla needs to “make room for increased Cybercab production.”.

It has been revealed that if the Cybertruck program was successful, Tesla wouldn’t be killing it. Tesla also produces Model Ys at Giga Texas, and it is not shutting that down to make room for Cybercab.

As we reported when Tesla declared the wind-down, that explanation doesn’t hold up. Giga Texas has more than 10 million square feet of floor space, the Cybertruck line runs at about a quarter of its 125,000-unit installed capacity, and Texas had only a few hundred Cybercabs registered as of late October.

In a recent development, the real problem is buyers. Tesla delivered 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3, and we estimated 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks, a pace of about 30,000 trucks a year. That was a good quarter by Cybertruck standards.

In a recent development, even that number flatters it. S&P Global Mobility data showed SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025, about 18% of US registrations that quarter. Tesla also tried a cheaper RWD trim, killed it, launched a $60,000 AWD version, then raised prices by $5,000 in August. None of it fixed demand.

I’ll give UP credit for this: the offer calls Musk’s bluff. If the Cybertruck is really dying because Cybercab needs the room, here’s someone volunteering to take the line off Tesla’s plate. Problem solved.

Of course, it’s more complicated than that.

There are many ways this could fail or never happen in the first place, but there’s also a slight possibility that makes this possible.

First off, the backlash is real. If you look on social media and forums, yes, most of the discussion is about how Cybertruck is a failure, and Elon is lying about why Tesla is killing it, but there’s also a serious group of people, especially Cybertruck owners, who are genuinely upset that Tesla is killing the program because they love their trucks.

Most people have never driven a Cybertruck, but the steer-by-wire makes it a very addictive vehicle to drive, and even though the price is high, the value proposition for the specs is not bad compared to the very limited options for electric pickup trucks.

In other words, I wouldn’t necessarily bet against this effort, especially if they add an SUV variant and show the program some love with some tweaks here and there.

Recent findings suggest that I could see a group of wealthy Cybertruck fans pooling money under Unplugged to make this happen, but getting Tesla to agree could be hard. It’s not unheard of for an automaker to sell a vehicle program to a dealer, like the Lotus Seven and Studebaker Avanti, but it would be a first at this scale.

In a recent development, who is singing up to light their cash on fire? There is just no way that would work. Unless Tesla just gave them the designs and tooling. Then they are stuck the same problem with who is their market. There are 3 ev trucks coming that are cheaper better and more practical. Likey 3 or 4 more by the end of the decade.

Recent findings suggest that you could make sense of it by looking at UP to Tesla as AMG to Mercedes. It’s not too big a stretch, considering UP isn’t just your average Tesla tuner. It even worked with the automaker on its own version of the Model S Plaid.

If UP were to become for Tesla what AMG has become for Mercedes, it could make some sense for the manufacturer to run a separate vehicle program that started under Tesla, but even as I write this, I realize that there’s very little chance this will happen.

But I wish them the best of luck, and I would be happy to see the Cybertruck live on.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that SOCKS MAY BE an afterthought, but comfort starts from the ground up. Your feet carry you all day, and the right pair keeps them warm, dry, blister-free, and supported—whether you're running miles, commuting to the office, or dressing up in loafers. The best socks stay put, wick away moisture, prevent hot spots, and hold shape long after laundry day. And we would know: The Men’s Health team has been testing since 2018—well before the pandemic reset everyone’s wardrobe—wearing them to the gym, on hikes, across long travel days, and through weekend outings. Check out the criteria we considered, or use the table of contents to find your perfect pair.

For years, the Men's Health team has relied on Dickies for its solid, no-fuss, workwear-meets-streetwear styles. In addition to well-built work pants, the brand's socks can go toe-to-toe (get it?) with just about every pair on the market, too. The fabric blend—71% cotton, 27% polyester, and 2% spandex—is an amazing trifecta, meaning they’re moisture-wicking, quick-drying, and odor-resistant. Plus, a little stretch goes a long way, ensuring the sock moves with you, not against you.

We found they're incredibly comfortable for casual wear and working out, thanks to their performance technology and superior arch support. They hit that perfect middle ground—they're not super thick, but they're not paper-thin either. There's enough cushioning without making your feet feel bulky or overheated.

Many of our testers didn't mind wearing them with boots, since the ventilation channels keep air flowing around the clock. That remarked, they really come in handy for guys on their feet 24/7—construction workers, mechanics, warehouse personnel, etc. No slipping, no bunching, just all-day support. As for the price, it’s hard to complain when you can stock up on three packs for under $50.

Recent findings suggest that these socks from Mack Weldon look cool in a way that works just as well with a suit as with jeans and sneakers. Besides looking nice, the best part about these socks is their odor-fighting properties. Mack Weldon infused the Pima cotton with silver fibers that are naturally antimicrobial. They're using a little basic chemistry to keep your feet smelling good all day. We also love how they stay on and won't slide down, even after a whole day of wear, thanks to the stay-put cuff on these socks.

Industry observers note that in our testing, we found that Mack Weldon’s crew socks are also great for walking, thanks to their cushioned footbed. The extended length provides extra coverage and warmth for your legs on cooler days, too. And since both the toe and heel are seamless and the fabric is ultra-soft, the comfort of these socks will keep your legs and feet feeling good all day long.

It has been revealed that there isn't a sock quite like a Gold Toe. These updated classics, for instance, are made from a slightly thick blend of wool and nylon, and boast AquaFX Moisture Control that helps wick away sweat throughout the coverage area to help you stay fresh, cool, and dry. The ribbed construction also provides extra support and warmth, while the stretch will help the socks fit perfectly on your feet. We also love the reinforced toe that ensures no hole, wear, or tear will happen for a long time.

In a recent development, in my testing, I found that while these indeed are cushy and warm—and thus work great as winter socks—they are quite thick, which is why I love wearing them to fill up the space in my boots or dress shoes, but sometimes for sneakers and athletic shoes, the thickness can feel very tight. And unlike other socks, these don’t slide down even on large calf muscles.

It has been revealed that no-show socks exist for one simple reason: to give you that clean, sockless look without the sweaty, blister-filled nightmare of actually going sockless. Enter this athletic, moisture-wicking pair made with Coolmax fiber, which helps keep perspiration in check when you're cycling, lifting, or running. Speaking of those activities, we also appreciate the seamless toe closure to prevent yarn chafing and discomfort while on the move. Aside from sport use, we found them to offer durability and excellent cushioning for casual wear. Bonus: Mesh ventilation on the instep ensures superb breathability from toe to heel. Plus, the three-pack is available in a variety of bold color pairings (orange, green, and blue).

Ask any sock aficionado their favorite sock brand, and there's a good chance they’ll say Bombas. According to recent reports, on top of that, it’s made with seamless toe construction to eliminate pressure points, and even a little fabric tab at the back to prevent pesky, painful blisters. Plus, the honeycomb support system gives your arch a snug, supportive hug—keeping your feet feeling secure and energized all day. The flex channels enhance mobility, meaning your socks move naturally with your foot instead of feeling restrictive, which is crucial when tackling uneven terrain on the trails. And the Y-shaped heel works hand-in-hand with these channels, creating a contoured, stay-put fit that keeps the sock in place.

In a recent development, great socks really come down to what they’re made of. The right material depends on where you’re wearing them and what you’re doing, whether that’s hitting the gym, heading to the office, going to a fancy dinner, or braving the elements.

Sources indicate that depending on your personal preference, the climate, the desired use, as well as your own feet, both thin and thick socks have their own advantages. Thin socks are usually more breathable and better at wicking away sweat and are thus great for combating foot odor. Thin socks are also preferred for warm weather. On the other hand, thick socks are your winter socks, providing better insulation and warmth. Thick socks often have better underfoot cushioning and padding as well, meaning they will help reduce friction in shoes or during long walks. Thick socks can sometimes add an entire size to your feet and make your shoe-wearing experience much more unbearable—unless you always size up for footwear, not to mention overheat your feet.

Industry observers note that keep in mind that socks that are too thin might not lend adequate protection, leading to blisters and foot pain. We recommend midweight socks because they can provide a good balance of comfort and support. A sock's thickness also denotes its weight, which is very personal. Some people like a heavier-weight sock with cushion to wear with a casual or lug sole shoe while others prefer a lighter-weight sock with their oxfords or loafers.

Sock height changes how your whole outfit reads and how your socks actually perform. The rise determines how much skin you’re showing (or not), how well your legs are protected, and whether your proportions look intentional or off. In other words: height matters. The “right” sock height ultimately comes down to personal taste—but it should always make sense with your shoes. Think about the shoes you’re wearing, the break of your pants (or shorts), and how much coverage you actually want. The right sock height can sharpen your proportions, prevent awkward gaps, and make the whole fit feel polished. When the proportions are off, the whole look feels off. Here’s how the main heights break down:.

Sources indicate that the best socks let your feet stay cool and breathable throughout the workday. Which is why you should preferably look for socks with moisture-wicking, arguably the most important feature in socks. Having moisture-wicking socks is extra crucial if you're wearing them for sports, long walks, or any hardcore outdoor activities because wicking away sweat and keeping your feet dry are keys to reducing the risk of blisters and fungal infections.

Industry observers note that we’ve been testing socks since 2018, and over the years, the Men’s Health team has rotated through more than 50 pairs across daily commutes, heavy leg days, long-haul flights, winter hikes, and 20,000-step city weekends. If a sock slid down, trapped sweat, thinned out at the heel, or lost its shape after a few washes, it didn’t make this list.

We evaluated what actually matters in real life: comfort, breathability, durability, and fit. That meant paying close attention to materials—soft but sturdy cotton for everyday wear, moisture-wicking synthetics that hold up in the gym, and Merino wool that regulates temperature without overheating. Construction was non-negotiable. We looked for seamless toes that prevent rubbing, supportive arch bands that don’t feel restrictive, and cuffs that stay put without strangling your calves. And because socks shouldn’t fall apart after a season, we repeatedly washed and wore each pair to make sure they didn’t sag, pill, or thin out at the heel and toe.

We also tapped menswear expert Ted Stafford, who has styled countless MH covers and editorial shoots, to weigh in on proportion, height, and how socks should work with everything from tailored trousers to retro sneakers.

Recent findings suggest that A weekend getaway is all the better with the right duffel—preferably one that meets your wife’s every packing need without weighing her (or your car) down. Enter Etronik. Sources indicate that these cozy memory foam loafers are a low-key treat your wife will actually wear around the house and after workouts. The plush lining hugs her feet, and the cushy insole gives just the right support for lounging or light errands.

A diamond necklace doesn’t have to be an anniversary-only purchase. The simple round solitaire is a foolproof choice, and opting for a lab-grown diamond keeps the cost down, even at a full carat. Check whether she usually wears yellow or white metals, then choose the finish to match.

Industry observers note that that favorite photo of you two deserves better than getting buried in her camera roll. Turn it into a keepsake with this brass-and-glass ornament, which includes a double-sided print, then then add the optional year tag to mark the occasion.

Industry News: 5 New Retail Design Rules, According to Experts

📅 06 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when nearly anything can be bought with a few taps on a screen, brick-and-mortar stores have to work harder—and smarter—to earn a visit.
  • The first goal for any newly introduced retail space is obvious: Make people want to be there.
  • Sources indicate that fashion designer Danielle Frankel Hirsch just opened a 12,000-square-foot studio in Tribeca, collaborating with Studio Partners Architecture and AD PRO Directory designer Augusta Hoffman to create a gasp-worthy dress boutique worthy of any bride's fantasies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when nearly anything can be bought with a few taps on a screen, brick-and-mortar stores have to work harder—and smarter—to earn a visit. What e-commerce can't replicate, even with the cleverest algorithms, is the thrill of stepping into a beautifully conceived space—and discovering something you didn't know you wanted. From side-by-side jewel-box fashion boutiques in Paris to a palatial bridal studio set in a 19th-century building in downtown Upcoming York, AD PRO highlights the big ideas shaping today’s most engaging retail environments.

The first goal for any newly introduced retail space is obvious: Make people want to be there.

Sources indicate that fashion designer Danielle Frankel Hirsch just opened a 12,000-square-foot studio in Tribeca, collaborating with Studio Partners Architecture and AD PRO Directory designer Augusta Hoffman to create a gasp-worthy dress boutique worthy of any bride's fantasies. Located in a 19th century edifice originally built to house the Upcoming York Mercantile Exchange, the shop, notes Frankel Hirsch, is designed as a transportive experience. After guests enter the space through its unassuming Tribeca storefront entrance, they ascend a grand carpeted staircase to a large gallery boasting over 30-foot floor-to-ceiling windows. Hoffman worked with artist Miriam Ellner to create églomisé paneling surrounding the staircase, and outfitted the spaces to the height of elegance, with Fortuny fabrics, furniture sourced from Paris, and handpainted ceiling murals.

The 30-foot ceilings at Latest York City's Danielle Frankel guarantee a wedding dress shopping experience that's hard to equal.

Recent findings suggest that in Paris, Rubirosa's two petite boutiques, designed by Louis Charles Aka, deliver a similar sense of occasion on a much smaller scale. The original 500-square-foot shop, which opened in June 2025, was joined this past August by a second location just next door. Rather than simply duplicate the first boutique's nostalgic formality, Aka has given its newly introduced neighbor a distinct personality. The lacquered shelving remains, displaying cashmere sweaters, crisp poplin shirts, and soft leather slippers in a rainbow of colors. But where the original featured tall bookcases, the new shop has floor-to-ceiling arches whose cubbies become bands of color when filled with garments of cashmere, cotton, and silk.

It has been revealed that in the original boutique, the defining gesture was a dense, velvety red wall-to-wall carpet from La Maison Bineau. “I spent everything on the red carpet,” Aka declares. “People criticized, ‘You will have to change it in three months.’ I said, ‘We don’t care. We want people to feel special.’” In the second shop, the color drama comes courtesy of vivid Yves Klein blue—a knowing wink to the fashion set. Voluminous white balloon drapery heightens the theatricality, suggesting a salon for elegant grand dames even as the boutique attracts a younger crowd of influencers and trendsetters.

Lacquered walls hung with portraits of Pope John Paul II and Mobutu Sese Seko at Rubirosa’s.

The exterior of Rubirosa’s on Rue de Grenelle in Paris.

According to recent reports, AD100 designer Brigette Romanek took a more subtle approach to creating desire at Catherine Bloom for Nordstrom, an appointment-only shop in Los Angeles where Bloom, the department store’s Director of Luxury Styling, works with private clients. “I want to make people feel something,” says Romanek. “A store should be a destination you look forward to.” Her use of paneled walls in camel, khaki, and rose suede, plus her signature mix of elements both edgy (the angular leather sofa) and delicate (the plasterwork ceiling) creates what she calls “a protected feeling” that makes the space feel worth seeking out.

Suede-paneled walls and ornate plasterwork at Catherine Bloom for Nordstrom.

A punchy red-orange “wallop” moment at Substantial Night’s West Village outpost.

In a recent development, where Romanek’s space whispers intimacy, Katherine Lewin’s Major Night shouts joy. The Newly introduced York City shop Big Night, which sells brightly hued kitchen and entertaining goods, trades old-world refinement for modern exuberance. “People tell me they get a shot of serotonin walking into the store,” she states. Her brand’s signature color of punchy red-orange provides what she calls a “wallop”—an immediate sensory experience that registers before customers even process what they’re looking at. Handmade tiles from Smink Studio, screen-printed with bold geometric patterns, are mixed in unexpected color combinations throughout the West Village store.

FoundRae’s Aspen boutique, complete with velvety chairs, books, and intriguing display cases lined with handwritten letters, old photos, and found objects.

It has been revealed that once you’ve lured customers in, the next challenge is keeping them there. “If someone is waiting for their partner to try on 50 things, they need to be comfortable,” states Romanek, who installed upholstered chairs from her collection for Crate & Barrel inside individual dressing rooms. Meanwhile, curtains at the store stay closed at all times, enhancing the protected atmosphere that encourages clients to relax and take their time.

Beth Hutchens, founder of fine jewelry line FoundRae, has turned lingering into an art form. The average customer stay at her fine jewelry boutiques—which include locations in New York, Miami, Los Angeles, Dallas, Palm Beach, and Aspen—is an hour and a half. It makes sense when you consider the cozy reading nooks well stocked with books and a rotating menu of complimentary snacks and wine.

The maze-like layout of Substantial Night’s West Village.

In the age of algorithmic shopping recommendations, physical retail can offer something genuinely different: the pleasure of stumbling upon the unexpected. When Lewin found Big Night’s West Village location, for instance, it was a warren of small spaces and hidden corners that defied traditional notions of retail design. Rather than optimizing for efficient shopping (and increasing her renovation costs), she embraced the pre-existing layout and discovered that it primed shoppers’ sense of exploration and surprise. “The store feels like a house party with different things happening in different corners,” Lewin explains.

At Fishs Eddy's Brooklyn location, deliberately cluttered displays add to the sense of discovery.

Industry observers note that at Fishs Eddy, the beloved New York City housewares shop founded in 1986, the thrill of the hunt has always been part of the appeal. Now, four decades after opening its original Manhattan location, the retailer has expanded with two new outposts, at Chelsea Market and in Brooklyn's Dumbo neighborhood. The latter, an ambitious 3,800-square-foot space, deliberately preserves the cheerfully cluttered, homespun aesthetic that has become the brand's calling card. Rather than give the larger store a slick makeover, founder Julie Gaines embraced the same informal, decidedly human approach to retail design: Vintage-style dishes, deadstock dinnerware, and offbeat glassware are piled high on reclaimed-wood displays and mismatched vintage furniture, evoking the warehouses where the original merchandise was discovered. Gaines describes her merchandising philosophy as “very direct: the way we found it in the warehouse.” But that seemingly improvised look takes effort. “We spend a lot of time looking like we don’t spend time,” she admits. An old-fashioned soda fountain serving egg creams and inexpensive drip coffee adds to the new store's convivial atmosphere.

FoundRae takes discovery to remarkable lengths. Hutchens installed fully realized miniature vignettes behind unmarked cupboard doors—doll-size rooms that include recreations of her own home and FoundRae boutiques, complete with furniture and art. Display cases feature what Hutchens calls a “menagerie of the ephemeral”—handwritten letters, old photos, and evocative found items loosely pinned behind the jewelry. Then there are the “Discovery Drawers”—wood-fronted, glass-topped compartments that hold one-of-a-kind pieces unique to each location (never photographed or featured online).

Recent findings suggest that at Sézane’s upcoming 2,800-square-foot boutique on New York’s Upper East Side, designer Pierre Lacroix has created a similar element of surprise through a dramatic shift in mood. Dubbed L’Appartement on Madison Avenue, the space evokes a Parisian home crossed with an art gallery, with books, artwork by William Klein, and vintage furniture. Most of the boutique feels light and airy, with creamy walls, cerused oak parquet floors, and parchment light fixtures. But tucked off to one side is a small shoe salon, drenched in dark chocolate tones and moodily lit. The intimate, after hours lounge-like space offers an unexpected counterpoint to the rest of the shop.

Sézane’s newest shop, aka L’Appartement on Madison Avenue, designed by Pierre Lacroix.

The shoe salon at Sézane’s L’Appartement offers an unexpected change of atmosphere.

Even in Rubirosa’s tiny space, Aka has created moments of discovery. He’s filled the walls with oil portraits of Luciano Pavarotti, Pope John Paul II, and various international dictators—a quirky mix of imagery that gives the space a distinctive personality. Visual layers invite clients to continuously notice new details, rewarding repeat visits.

Wes Anderson calling! A particularly Instagrammable corner of Rubirosa’s.

Aka admits that Rubirosa’s Instagram-friendly storefront serves as what he calls “a lure”—beautiful enough that people stop to photograph it even if they don’t come inside. “Some people come just to take pictures in front,” he states. The combination of the crimson carpet, dark lacquered millwork, and those quirky framed portraits creates an irresistibly photogenic and TikTok-friendly environment. Romanek’s thoughtful color palette and material mix at the Nordstrom boutique creates a similarly camera-ready backdrop. The social media effect, says Romanek, is simply a natural byproduct of creating a distinctive space. “When a space feels different, conversations about it happen,” she explains. “And that’s what we like. We like people talking about the experience.”.

Industry observers note that at the Danielle Frankel bridal studio, the sheer spectacle reaches another level entirely. From the soaring ceilings to the grand staircase with its shimmering églomisé panels, the interiors offer no shortage of photo opportunities. But for a boutique devoted to dressing brides for what is, ideally, a once-in-a-lifetime occasion, perhaps a little over-the-top grandeur is exactly the point.

In a recent development, hoffman worked with the artist Miriam Ellner to create églomisé paneling surrounding the staircase. “The eglomise is one of my favorite things,” says Danielle Frankel designer Frankel Hirsch. The result is staircase that not creates a heightened emotional atmosphere for in-store shoppers but also provides a dramatic backdrop for photography.

Sources indicate that hutchens believes retail design isn’t inextricably tied to scalability. “Ask yourself, if every store was your only store, what would you do and how would you invest in it and change it?” she says. “You evolve faster when you think that way.”.

While all seven FoundRae stores share some design DNA—Hutchens embeds her signature mythological symbols in floors, ceilings, and furniture throughout—each reflects its location. The Aspen boutique is swathed in green, alluding to the town’s namesake aspen trees, with a large marquetry sunburst as its centerpiece. The Palm Beach shop features gilded verre églomisé, while in Miami, a vintage Steinway grand piano with hand-applied gold symbols anchors the room. As a result, the stores feel both part of a cohesive brand while rooted in their specific communities.

Substantial Night’s location in Brooklyn’s Greenpoint.

Substantial Night’s Upper East Side outpost.

Recent findings suggest that even Lewin’s three Big Night locations—Brooklyn, West Village, and the Upper East Side, which she calls “sisters, not twins”—each have distinct personalities while maintaining the brand’s joyful, color-saturated identity. Lewin likens the Upper East Side shop to a Classic Six apartment and notes that the upcoming millwork was designed to reflect an upscale, elevated home. Her cash desk placement in the West Village location, situated in the center of the largest room rather than tucked away, came from understanding that specific space and how her team could best interact with customers there.

The thread connecting these diverse approaches is a fundamental understanding that physical retail can no longer compete with e-commerce on convenience or selection. But the best retail spaces offer atmosphere, discovery, community, and the experience of being somewhere that feels genuinely special. As Aka puts it, “Like a good movie, when it ends...if you don’t have the feeling you want to see it again, it was not that good.”.

The back room of Rubirosa’s is painted in a pale baby blue, “like a boy’s little bedroom,” claims Aka. “So when you take out your credit card, it doesn’t bother you. It’s like you’re on a pillow.”.

A leather, steel, and palmwood sofa by Pacific Green at Catherine Bloom for Nordstrom, designed by AD100 talent Brigette Romanek.

It’s that time again – Honda needs to roll out an electric Super Cub

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub.
  • According to recent reports, the Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.

Recent findings suggest that I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub. Not another futuristic concept with swoopy bodywork and a name that looks like a Wi-Fi password. I mean an actual honest-to-goodness Honda Super Cub, except electric.

The formula is already sitting right there.

According to recent reports, the Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958. It’s still in continuous production today.

Industry observers note that and a huge part of that success comes down to how approachable the thing is. It isn’t supposed to be intimidating, excessively powerful, or particularly complicated. It’s simple, practical transportation wrapped in one of the most recognizable two-wheeler designs ever created.

In other words, it’s practically begging to become electric.

Recent findings suggest that the beauty of the bike is how simple and timeless it is, with the appearance barely changing in nearly 7 decades. And with the design freedom that electric drivetrains provide, upgrading the cute little bike to an electric future would be a walk in the park for Honda’s engineers.

An in-wheel motor would be a simple, cheap solution that frees up even more space in the body for batteries.

Sources indicate that and Honda wouldn’t need some enormous battery capable of highway touring. Give an electric Super Cub enough battery for perhaps 50-60 miles (80-95 km) of real-world urban riding, a motor capable of roughly 50-60 mph (80-95 km/h), and simple Level 1 charging from a normal wall outlet. As a city runabout or a beachside cruiser, those middle-of-the-road specs would be perfect.

Recent findings suggest that even better, make the battery removable. Honda already has its Mobile Power Pack e: swappable battery system used in various electric two-wheelers, and an electric Super Cub would be an incredible platform to expand it.

The resulting bike could hit an unusually sweet spot.

In a recent development, there are millions of people riding electric bicycles today who will eventually want something faster, but don’t necessarily want a 500-pound (220 kg) electric motorcycle capable of hitting 120 mph (200 km/h). An electric Super Cub would be a natural next step: light, unintimidating, easy to ride, cheap to operate, and fast enough to actually function as a real urban vehicle.

It would also be one of the rare electric motorcycles that could appeal to people who aren’t necessarily looking for an “electric motorcycle.” An electric version is in such high demand that companies specialize in retrofit kits to convert classic Cubs into EVs.

Recent findings suggest that the Super Cub already has decades of cultural cachet. It’s cute. It’s useful. It’s nostalgic without feeling ancient. It’s the kind of motorcycle that can appeal equally to a lifelong rider and someone who has never considered owning a motorcycle before.

Industry observers note that and perhaps most importantly, Honda could actually sell the thing globally. The same basic electric Super Cub could work in dense European cities, throughout Asia, and in American cities and suburbs. It doesn’t need to win spec-sheet battles. It just needs to be affordable, reliable, and unmistakably a Super Cub.

According to recent reports, my mum's old Honda-50 (the original cub, early 70's) had a tank that held less than a gallon of petrol. Range was realistically about 50 miles, but no-one even thought about that, it never ran out.

She traded for a honda-90, then a bunch of other stuff, I miss that 90, even now.

But the point is that range is not the concern, very few trips on these are more than 10 - 15 miles, say 30km round-trip.

But the real range, on a battery vehicle, is only about 2/3 of the claim,.

so if the claim is 80, it'll maybe do 55?

Thats enough, if it has the zip to handle traffic, and cruise at 45 - 50mph.

Honda has already shown that it understands the importance of electrifying small two-wheelers. It’s even made a token gesture with a Cub-like e-scooter in China. But there’s a difference between making another electric scooter and electrifying perhaps the most famous small motorcycle ever made.

So here I am once again, Honda.

It has been revealed that you’ve got the name. You’ve got the design. You’ve got the batteries. You’ve got the manufacturing scale.

According to recent reports, just put all the pieces together and give us the electric Super Cub already. The world is waiting, and will thank you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rosie Huntington-Whiteley returned to the Victoria's Secret runway this year after a 16-year hiatus, but the supermodel has continued to make fitness a priority throughout her career.

“It’s really about consistency because I’m a gym girl—I’m always training and taking care of myself,” Rosie told Vogue.

The former Burberry Body face has previously cited strength training as her main form of exercise.

“I feel really strong and it's improved my posture, muscle tone, and definition,” she said to Vogue on a separate occasion.

She recently shared a workout clip of herself doing an impressive upper-body exercise—the banded chin-up—just days before the show, writing: “No days off.”.

Chin-ups are a compound exercise targeting your back and arm muscles, including the latissimus dorsi (lats), biceps, and trapezius (traps).

A chin-up uses an underhand grip, with your palms facing you, while a pull-up uses an overhand grip, with your palms facing away.

Using a thicker band gives you more assistance when performing reps, while a thinner band gives you less.

Remember: while models' and celebrities' training routines can be inspiring, genetics also play a significant role in body shape, height and how easily someone builds muscle or stays lean. Take inspiration from the healthy habits – not the expectation of looking identical.

While the chin-up is a challenging movement, you can build up to your first bodyweight rep—without a band—using a few progression exercises.

Holding yourself above the bar keeps your muscles under constant tension, which helps build strength.

This exercise requires you to lower yourself as slowly as possible from the top of the movement. People are generally much stronger in the lowering phase of an exercise than in the lifting portion, making it easier than trying to pull yourself up. However, the movement still works your muscles throughout the entire range of motion, helping you build the strength needed to perform a chin-up.

Rosie has highlighted the importance of focusing on skill and feeling confident over aesthetics.

Industry observers note that “For me, it’s really about feeling strong and fit, as opposed to thinking about a number on the scales or on a measuring tape. Competence builds confidence,” she said.

Getting stronger brings her a sense of accomplishment.

Recent findings suggest that “There's nothing more satisfactory to me than when I go up in weight,” she added to Vogue. “It makes me happy when I start to see the results of [consistently] lifting.” In fact, regularly working out is “when [she] feels her strongest and fittest.”.

She added that motherhood had given her a new perspective on her body.

“I’m about to turn 40 next year; I look at my body and I have so much appreciation for having had two children,” Rosie continued.

It has been revealed that kate puts together fitness content that covers functional and strength training, cardio, workout challenges, interviews and news. She's often doing gym laundry or listening to music.
