#5692. The Best Electrolyte Powders, Tested by Registered Dietitians

📅 31 May 2024 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2488 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

The Best Electrolyte Powders, Tested by Registered Dietitians

📅 31 May 2024 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2488 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ELECTROLYTE POWDERS HAVE become very trendy over the last few years, but the variety of ingredients and numerous products on the market may leave you wondering what you actually need.
  • It has been revealed that the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) recommends a sodium intake of 300 to 600 milligrams per hour for endurance athletes who exercise for over two hours or are considered “heavy sweaters,” losing more than 1.2 liters per hour.
  • Recent findings suggest that as the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to find the latest and greatest equipment and supplements, including electrolyte powders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ELECTROLYTE POWDERS HAVE become very trendy over the last few years, but the variety of ingredients and numerous products on the market may leave you wondering what you actually need. These powders have various amounts of sodium and other electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium, etc.), plus sugars and additional ingredients meant to improve your hydration after a sweaty workout. Based on our extensive testing, we found that these formulas are an easy and convenient way to replenish electrolytes lost in sweat. That's because sweat contains water and electrolytes, with sodium losses being the highest, says Leah Reitmayer, MS, RD, a Board-Certified Sports Dietitian and owner of Lettuce Eat Dessert.

It has been revealed that the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) recommends a sodium intake of 300 to 600 milligrams per hour for endurance athletes who exercise for over two hours or are considered “heavy sweaters,” losing more than 1.2 liters per hour. Key: The average person doesn’t need an electrolyte supplement after your average one-hour workout. But when you need that extra boost of hydration and electrolyte replenishment, we have the seven best electrolyte powders to choose from, according to sports dietitians and athletes.

Recent findings suggest that as the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to find the latest and greatest equipment and supplements, including electrolyte powders. I personally tested each of these products in a variety of scenarios, including as part of a morning routine, in the afternoon after work, and after intense workouts, in the gym and on the track.

I also consulted Marty Munson, Health Director at Men’s Health, triathlete, and USA Triathlon Certified Coach; and Deputy Editor Paul Kita to get their insights on the electrolyte products they have tested throughout their years in the industry. Read on for our guide to the best electrolyte powders.

*Additional reporting by Kelsey Kunik, RDN.

Sources indicate that I’m a significant fan of Thorne because they design their supplements so that they can be used by the most elite athletes but are also accessible to everyone else. This formula provides a balanced blend of sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium. And in keeping with their no-BS approach, there aren’t any sweeteners, colors, or fillers, keeping the blend non-GMO and gluten-free.

Sources indicate that poured into the glass, the powder dissolves promptly and completely, leaving only the color and refreshing taste. I’m a fan of the flavors, which they kept to three heavy-hitters, and if you’re not picky, I recommend the variety pack so you can switch between them.

Sources indicate that we’ve seen that brands have been smartly moving away from carbohydrate formulas, so that you can customize your carb intake if you’re an athlete. That is the case here, with only a single gram of carbs. So if you’re looking for a quality, easy-to-drink electrolyte powder that can also travel with you, this is the best.

According to recent reports, transparent Labs Hydrate electrolyte powder includes multiple electrolytes and other nutrients like taurine and Senactiv, an adaptogen complex that supports muscle recovery. “It has 500 mg of sodium per serving, which fits ACSM’s recommendation for sodium replacement per hour,” says registered dietitian Sarah Alsing, MS, RD. You’ll also replace small amounts of potassium, magnesium, and calcium.

Sources indicate that each dose has 1,000 milligrams of taurine, a sulfur-containing amino acid that may help support muscle recovery. You can choose from six flavors, all sweetened with stevia, as this formula is carbohydrate and calorie-free.

According to recent reports, “I look for supplements to be third-party tested so you can trust the ingredients listed, and Transparent Labs is third-party tested,” says Alsing. It’s Informed Sport Certified, meaning it’s been tested for substances banned by major athletic regulating organizations, which gives peace of mind to competing athletes.

This electrolyte powder only comes in a multi-serving tub, which could be seen as a downside if you want to take your electrolytes on the road often. But for us, it is a great way to reduce waste and if you’re taking electrolytes as part of your daily routine, you’re probably usually taking them at home.

Industry observers note that experts and testers we consulted with say LMNT is a serious electrolyte supplement, providing 1,000 milligrams of sodium in each pack. With this much salt, you can expect the flavor to be, well, salty. After a 10-mile run or a hard, sweaty bike ride, we appreciate the replenishment, but the salty flavor may take a little getting used to for some people. However, other athletes like Munson actually prefer that taste over some typical sports drinks, which can taste overly sweet. Personally, I tend to agree. The instructions include mixing a packet with 16 to 32 ounces of water, but you can always dilute it a little more to cut the salty flavor. I drink mine with about 12 ounces of water, and find the salty taste to be a bit stronger but still enjoyable at these proportions.

It has been revealed that “There are several flavors to choose from, which helps finding one you will enjoy and tolerate during your workouts,” indicates Alsing. You can choose from fruit flavors like citrus or watermelon or even a more decadent chocolate caramel. It’s sweetened with stevia leaf, and one packet has just 2 grams of carbohydrates. If you don’t like the taste of stevia, you can always choose the raw, unflavored option with no sweeteners added. Personally, I stick to the fruity flavors as I feel the salty taste is best when combined with citrus, berry, or melon notes.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to sodium, LMNT provides 200 milligrams of potassium and 60 milligrams of magnesium, electrolytes that are also lost through sweat, although in lower amounts than sodium. Personally, I find that drinking these electrolytes right in the morning keeps me better hydrated throughout the day.

Read more: Best Supplements for Men.

Sources indicate that not only is Nuun Sport Powder certified gluten-free, but this product is also vegan and kosher. The Nuun tablets are effervescent, which can be difficult to drink while running or biking. But the Sport Electrolyte Tablets have no fizz, making it a better option for athletes drinking them on the go. The powder sticks come in five flavors and have just one gram of added sugars along with stevia for a sweet flavor. While many people love the packet flavors, they are a lot stronger than the tablets, which may be off-putting for some athletes if you’re drinking them during a workout.

In a recent development, each packet has 300 milligrams of sodium, along with potassium and magnesium, making it a good all-around hydration drink for workouts lasting an hour or less. The packets are easy to tear and mix quickly into a water bottle for hydration on the go—no waiting for tablets to dissolve. And while Nuun is known more for their tablets, we find the powder packets to be the superior form when it comes to mid-workout hydration.

This formula has 330 milligrams of sodium in each serving and is free from gluten, soy, and certified vegan. This formula does have 7 grams of added sugars and a total of 9 grams of carbohydrates but is also one of the few that does not use stevia as a sweetener. Though 7 grams of sugar is higher than zero-sugar brands, it’s a lot less than some competitors use (for example, Liquid I.V. has 11 grams of added sugar per serving).

And unlike the other powders, this one has 15 percent DV of zinc, an essential trace mineral that helps with the absorption of water and electrolytes by the intestines, aiding hydration.If you’re looking for a zero sugar option, they have the Zero Sugar Variety which also has the addition of several B vitamins.

Liquid I.V. has been in the electrolyte game a while, but their original product contains 11 grams of added sugar. To keep up with competitors boasting formulas sans sugar, they released a sugar-free line and it does not disappoint. This updated formula is one of our favorite sugar-free electrolyte powders on the market, sweetened instead with stevia and allulose (a naturally occurring, low-calorie sugar that doesn’t spike blood glucose).

According to recent reports, each stick delivers 500 milligrams of sodium, which meets ACSM’s recommendations and is ideal for heavy sweaters or endurance athletes. You’ll also get 370 milligrams of potassium, but you won’t find any magnesium or calcium in this product—which could be a miss for those looking for a complete electrolyte supplement rather than the heavily sodium-focused product here.

It has been revealed that it’s worth noting that Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free does contain vitamin C, niacin, and B vitamins, added micronutrients that many electrolyte supplements do not offer. This formula mixes easily into water and comes in unique flavors like white peach and rainbow sherbet. Just be aware that the sweetening agent allulose, while generally well-tolerated, may cause mild bloating or gas in some people.

First and foremost, not everyone needs an electrolyte powder (or an electrolyte drink) every day. In fact, the average American is getting way too much sodium in their diet, contributing to chronic health conditions like heart disease and high blood pressure. “The average man working out for an hour a day can meet their electrolyte needs through what they eat and should prioritize drinking plenty of water,” says Alsing. She recommends eating potassium-rich foods like bananas, avocados, and potatoes, and salty foods like salted nuts or pickles after a sweaty workout.

If you’re unsure whether you would benefit from an electrolyte powder, talk with a registered dietitian, or try a product like the Nix Hydration Biosensor, which measures your sweat output in real time. Marty Munson—Health Director at Men’s Health, triathlete, and USA Triathlon Certified Coach—says sweat testing played a significant role in helping her customize a rehydration initiative. For those who have done the research, talked to their doctors, and are sweating more than most recreational athletes, we’ve got the scoop (pun intended) on what to look for in the best electrolyte supplements below.

“You want to look for a product that contains at least 230-690mg of sodium,” indicates Reitmayer. This is in line with the ACSM recommendations to replace sodium losses after two hours of exercise or exercise that results in heavy sweating. Losing just 1 to 2 percent of your body weight through sweat can lead to an increased heart rate, higher core temperature, as well as decreased cardiac output, time to exhaustion, and power. Sodium helps maintain fluid retention in the body, leading to less water loss and improved hydration status as you drink water to replace what you lost through sweat.

Sources indicate that electrolyte powders vary widely in sugar content. We recommend looking for options with no more than 5 to 10 grams of added sugar unless you’re using it as both a hydration and carbohydrate source during longer workouts. For casual training or daily hydration, sugar-free options using stevia, monk fruit, or allulose are usually preferred. Be mindful of sugar alcohols, which can cause bloating or GI discomfort in some people.

If you want to combine your carbohydrate refueling and electrolytes in one drink, look for a formula that has a carbohydrate source. Munson explains that the trend is going away from these types of drinks, as many athletes like to have more control over their refueling source, choosing a separate powder for electrolytes and using other mixes, gels, or chews as an energy source. Some electrolyte powders have no carbohydrates, while others may contain 15 grams or more. “If you are looking for a sports drink with electrolytes, aim for 5-10% of the solution carbohydrates,” claims Reitmayer.

According to recent reports, sodium isn’t the only electrolyte lost through sweat, even though it is the most abundant. You may also want an electrolyte powder that replaces electrolytes like potassium, magnesium, chloride, and/or zinc. While it’s helpful to replace these electrolytes as well, some athletes prefer less magnesium, as forms of this mineral can have a slight laxative effect, which you would probably want to avoid while competing.

Industry observers note that how you strategy to use your electrolyte powder should factor into the packaging you choose. Single-serving sticks or packets are great for travel, races, or throwing in your gym bag. They’re lightweight, easy to portion, and reduce mess when you’re on the move. Multi-serving tubs can be more cost-effective and environmentally friendly, but they require measuring and aren’t as convenient mid-workout or on the trail. Either way, look for resealable, moisture-resistant packaging to keep the powder fresh and free from clumping.

Electrolyte powders can be used before, during, and after exercise to help replace fluids lost during periods of long exercise or heavy sweating.

Recent findings suggest that replacing water and sodium helps to avoid the effects of dehydration, which could include an increase in heart rate, core temperature, and muscle glycogen use and a decrease in cardiac output, cognitive awareness, anaerobic power, and time to exhaustion. All of these can have negative effects on performance.

Industry observers note that any exercise where you’re sweating can lead to electrolyte losses. Short sweat sessions can usually be replaced with the sodium included in regular foods and drinks, while sessions longer than two hours may need a stronger source of sodium, like an electrolyte rehydration drink.

According to recent reports, depending on the ingredients, some electrolyte powders could lead to digestive upset, especially if they include high amounts of sugar, sugar alcohol, or magnesium. Drinking electrolyte powders when you’re not losing sodium through sweat or if you have high blood pressure could increase your blood pressure.

#5690. Ice Dives Are the Simple Therapy Trick that Rewired My Anxious Brain

Ice Dives Are the Simple Therapy Trick that Rewired My Anxious Brain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A few weeks ago, I was more anxious than I had been in a long time—or maybe ever.
  • While calling your sister is always a good idea, mine also happens to be a clinical fellow at McLean Hospital, a.k.a.
  • “I’m not hanging up until you do it,” she said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A few weeks ago, I was more anxious than I had been in a long time—or maybe ever. My thoughts were racing, and even for someone who deals with her share of anxiety, I was way beyond my normal self. So, I did what any person would do in that moment: I called my sister.

While calling your sister is always a good idea, mine also happens to be a clinical fellow at McLean Hospital, a.k.a. one of the leading psychiatric institutions in the whole country, so let’s just say she knows how to handle an anxious person. Her suggestion was to go to the kitchen, grab a massive bowl, fill it with ice water, and then dunk my face in it. I wasn’t exactly thrilled by the idea. It seemed like a whole bunch of work for something that couldn’t possibly help me in such a state.

“I’m not hanging up until you do it,” she said. She could tell I thought the idea was silly, and that I was probably going to skip it. And, I did think it was silly, but she seemed weirdly passionate that I submerge my face into a bowl of freezing water, so I complied. I grabbed a bowl, filled it with water and ice cubes, and reluctantly got my face wet, just barely making sure my nose and eyes were underwater.

In a recent development, I felt better basically instantly. The racing thoughts subsided and I could finally see straight. Even more impressive is the fact that once I reentered the situation that was making me anxious, all that nervous energy simply didn’t return. I was reset and relaxed. All it took was a bucket of water and about 30 seconds.

The trick—or, skill, I should say—that my sister taught me comes from dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT), a modality that was created by Marsha Linehan, PhD, who recently passed away at 83 years old. It was a breakthrough treatment for people facing extreme mental health challenges like chronic suicidality and borderline personality disorder, which Linehan revealed she struggled with in 2011, decades after DBT became the gold standard for treating those conditions.

Recent findings suggest that whether or not you are someone who deals with a formal mental health diagnosis or the occasional tough moment, DBT skills can make a big difference. The cold water trick my sister taught me is called an “ice dive,” and it’s one of four simple DBT tools that can help snap you out of a range of intense emotions swiftly. Now, any time I feel myself getting heightened, my immediate next thought is: I should go grab a bucket of ice water. Call me converted.

Here’s how you can practice this skill too, plus, the three others that work just as well—and don’t involve water.

Meet the experts: Shireen Rizvi, PhD, is a clinical psychologist and director of psychology training and DBT services and research at Montefiore Einstein in New York City. Vibh Forsythe Cox, PhD, is a clinical associate professor at the University of Washington and the director of the Marsha M. Linehan DBT clinic.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, you’ve pretty much gotten the entire gist of an ice dive, but let’s recap: All it takes is a bowl big enough to get your full face in and some chilly water. (The colder the better, but it doesn’t need to reach ice bath territory.) Once you’ve got that, place it on a low-set table or even on the ground—you want to be bending over when you dunk your head in to mimic something closer to a dive—take a deep breath, and submerge your face, especially around your nasal passages and eyes, for as long as possible. 30 seconds is ideal, but that may feel like a really long time at first. Just go for as long as you can, and feel free to repeat multiple times for a cumulative total of 30 seconds.

As for what is going on when you do this: Dunking your face in cold water triggers what is called the mammalian dive reflex, says Shireen Rizvi, PhD, a clinical psychologist and director of psychology training and DBT services and research at Montefiore Einstein in Upcoming York City. “It’s automatic,” she says. “You’re not doing anything consciously to create the reaction, which is there to help mammals survive cold water.”.

An ice dive triggers a survival mode where our bodies reduce our heart rate, slow down our breathing, and redirect blood to our vital organs, she explains. Under water, it helps you stay alive, but on land, it helps calm just about any activating emotion you might be experiencing. And, your face being what’s submerged is critical to get this specific reaction; getting in an ice bath where your face isn’t underwater actually spikes your heart rate due to cold shock, for example.

Basically, an ice dive forces your body to focus on the bare necessities, like staying calm. It’s best used anytime your emotions are reaching a 90-plus on a scale of 1 to 100, Rizvi claims, whether the emotion is anxiety, anger, stress, jealousy, or anything else. If you’re feeling it intensely and your heart rate is up, an ice dive can help.

According to recent reports, there’s one other handy use case too: If you’re ruminating. “When your body is in a survival mode, it's pulling resources back, and it actually also pulls your attention too, so if you have a lot of thoughts floating around in your head making you anxious, this can also help clear your mind temporarily,” states Vibh Forsythe Cox, PhD, a clinical associate professor at the University of Washington and the director of the Marsha M. Linehan DBT clinic. Think of it this way: “You can't be thinking about a grocery list if you have just fallen into ice water,” she says.

And, while this trick has completely changed the game for me, I have some good news: There are three others that all have the same effect sans H2O.

An ice dive makes up the very first letter—T for temperature—in the TIPP acronym, which is a part of DBT’s distress tolerance pillar. The rest (intense exercise, paced breathing, and paired muscle relaxation) can all swiftly calm and reset your nervous system, no liquid necessary.

All four skills have a similar basic mechanism. They take you from a heightened state (or a distressed one, to use DBT-speak) where your sympathetic nervous system is activated and bring you back into a relaxed one, where your parasympathetic nervous system is in the driver’s seat again. They’re not about talking or reflecting; they’re about helping you feel better in a moment when emotions are extreme.

Recent findings suggest that “These are skills that act to regulate your physiology,” Cox notes. “Oftentimes when you are having an intense emotion, you think you have to handle it with your mind. These are skills that help you handle it with your body.” Of course, once you’re out of that intense moment, you may want to call on other mental tools and process what happened—but that’s not where you’re at when you’re calling on a TIPP skill. They’re for when you’re in crisis mode.

You can use any of them at any time with one notable caveat: All TIPP skills are meant to rapidly slow down your heart rate, so if you’re someone with a heart condition or who takes meds like beta blockers, talk to your doctor first before trying any of them, Rizvi claims.

Without further ado, here’s what you need to know about the other three skills.

Sources indicate that the I in TIPP stands for intense exercise. This may sound similarly prohibitive to needing a bowl of water, but it’s actually quite simple. All you really need to do is get moving for about 30 seconds. Do some all-out jumping jacks, pump your arms up and down as fast as you can while sitting in your chair, or get into a plank. Just get your heart rate up and your muscles feel fatigued. “It feels paradoxical, but when you end that short burst of exercise, everything slows down,” Rizvi states.

Sources indicate that there’s also an added benefit to going with exercise. When you’re feeling a heightened emotion, one of the ways your sympathetic nervous system reacts is by sending out glucose into your bloodstream, Cox says. Again, this is an automatic, physical reaction, and it’s what gives you the energy for either a fight or flight response. But since you're probably not feeling anxious or angry because you need to escape a pack of hungry wolves, you probably won’t end up literally running away or fighting them off and using that energy. Exercising eats up some of that extra glucose, helping you get back to baseline.

Sources indicate that if you’ve ever done box breathing, you’ve done the first P in TIPP. All it involves is breathing in and out in a controlled manner for a set number of seconds each time. “The main core of this technique is that your out breath needs to be longer than your in breath,” notes Cox. “That is what activates your parasympathetic nervous system and slows everything down.”.

In addition to keeping your out breath longer than your in breath (say four seconds in and eight out), you also want to make sure you’re breathing from your diaphragm, Rizvi says. You can monitor this by placing your hand on your belly. If it’s rising and falling with each breath, you’re breathing from your diaphragm.

If you’re looking for an entry-level DBT skill, or one that you can do in pretty much any context, this is a good one to master. “I find paced breathing in particular is something that you can usually do no matter where you are or what you're doing,” Rizvi says. It takes no setup, no resources, and you can even do it in plain sight without people noticing.

Finally, the last TIPP skill is paired muscle relaxation. “When we are having an intense emotion, our body tenses up,” Cox says. “This helps release some of that tension.”.

Sources indicate that to do this skill, start at one end of your body and systematically work your way up or down, tensing and releasing your muscles throughout and saying the word “relax” each time. Pairing the muscle tensing with the word relax also helps train them—and therefore you—to relax on command, Cox says.

There are plenty of guided paired muscle relaxation routines you can follow online, but you can also just do it on your own, tensing as many muscle groups as you’d like (or have time for).

Don’t have time to reread an article in a moment of crisis? Here are the quick and simple basics of all the TIPP skills for when you need to use them ASAP.

Sources indicate that no matter which one you go for, remember this: “Emotions fire in the order of milliseconds,” Cox states. That means that no matter how intense the thing you’re feeling is, it will pass, and probably much faster than you think. Sometimes, all our brains need is a reset initiated by our bodies.

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

It has been revealed that the award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 new models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

The judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

Kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Launched in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

It has been revealed that it’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, debuted in May, outperformed the newly introduced Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”.

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

What Are Perpetual Futures? How Crypto's Most Popular Derivative Works

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Perpetual futures are the engine room of crypto trading.
  • They aren't only for crypto, either.
  • This guide explains what futures are, what makes perpetual futures different, how funding rates and liquidations work, and what to know before trading them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Perpetual futures are the engine room of crypto trading. Centralized exchanges processed $85.3 trillion in perps trading volume in 2025 alone, according to CoinGecko's State of Crypto Perpetuals Report 2026, and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) describes perps as the dominant form of crypto derivatives trading.

They aren't only for crypto, either. Exchanges now offer perps on stocks, commodities and currencies, and Decrypt has become the first news publisher to offer perps trading, powered by Solana exchange Phoenix.

This guide explains what futures are, what makes perpetual futures different, how funding rates and liquidations work, and what to know before trading them.

To understand perpetual futures, it helps to start with ordinary futures.

It has been revealed that A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a set date in the future. Futures have been used for centuries: farmers used them to lock in prices for crops before harvest, and today they are traded on everything from oil and wheat to stock indexes and Bitcoin, on regulated exchanges such as CME.

Sources indicate that traders use futures for two main reasons. Hedgers use them to protect against price swings; an airline might buy oil futures to lock in fuel costs, for example. Speculators use them to bet on price movements without owning the underlying asset.

Recent findings suggest that traditional futures have an expiry date. When a contract expires, it settles, either by delivering the asset or, more often, by paying out the difference in cash. Traders who want to keep their position open must "roll" it into a new contract, which can add costs and complexity.

Perpetual futures, often shortened to "perps" or "perpetual swaps," work like futures, but with one key difference: they never expire. Traders can hold a position for as long as they like, provided they have enough collateral to keep it open.

It has been revealed that the idea was proposed by Yale economist Robert Shiller in a 1993 paper as a way to create markets for assets that are hard to trade directly. Perps took off in crypto. Crypto exchange BitMEX, widely credited with bringing perps to crypto, launched a perpetual contract on Bitcoin in 2016. BitMEX itself closed in September 2026, but the product it pioneered has become the most traded instrument in crypto.

According to recent reports, A perpetual contract never actually involves owning the asset. Traders deposit collateral, or "margin," and their profit or loss depends entirely on how the price moves.

It has been revealed that when opening a perp position, a trader chooses a direction. Going long means betting the price will rise; going short means betting it will fall. Being able to short as easily as going long is one reason perps are popular: it lets traders profit from falling prices, or hedge assets they already own.

Perps are usually traded with leverage, which lets traders control a larger position than their collateral alone would allow. With 10x leverage, for example, $100 of margin controls a $1,000 position. If the asset's price rises 5%, the trader makes $50, a 50% return on their margin. But if it falls 5%, they lose $50, half of their margin.

It has been revealed that exchanges track two prices to manage this. The index price is the asset's price on spot markets, usually averaged across several exchanges. The mark price, based on the index and the perp market itself, is used to calculate profits and losses and to decide when positions must be closed. Using an averaged price makes it harder for a sudden spike on one exchange to trigger liquidations.

Industry observers note that because perps never expire, nothing forces their price to converge with the underlying asset, as traditional futures do at expiry. Instead, perps use a funding rate.

At regular intervals—most commonly every eight hours, though some platforms use shorter or longer schedules—traders on one side of the market pay traders on the other:.

Decentralized exchange Hyperliquid, for example, pays funding every hour, at one-eighth of the rate calculated for an eight-hour period, to stay consistent with centralized exchanges.

Funding payments go directly between traders, not to the exchange. For traders holding positions over long periods, these payments can add up, and they can either boost or erode returns.

Funding rates also offer a window into market sentiment. Strongly positive funding suggests traders are crowded into bullish bets, while negative funding shows that bears are paying to stay short.

Rates for the same asset can also differ between exchanges. On November 19, 2026, Bitcoin's funding rate was 0.01% per eight hours on Hyperliquid, compared with 0.0037% on Binance, according to Hyperliquid's funding comparison tool.

Some traders aim to earn funding payments rather than bet on prices. In a "cash and carry" or basis trade, they buy an asset on the spot market and short the same amount through perps, collecting funding while their positions offset each other's price moves.

Industry observers note that leverage is a double-edged sword. Every perp position has a maintenance margin, the minimum collateral needed to keep it open. If losses push a trader's margin below that level, the exchange automatically closes the position, a process called liquidation. The trader typically loses most or all of the margin they put up.

Sources indicate that the higher the leverage, the smaller the price move needed to trigger a liquidation. At 50x leverage, a 2% move against a position can wipe it out.

Industry observers note that liquidations can also feed on each other. When prices fall sharply, liquidated longs are forced to sell, pushing prices lower and triggering further liquidations, a so-called liquidation cascade. On October 10, 2025, the crypto market saw its largest liquidation event on record, with more than $19 billion in leveraged positions wiped out in a single day.

Recent findings suggest that to cover losses when positions can't be closed in time, exchanges typically keep an insurance fund. In extreme cases, some use auto-deleveraging, closing profitable positions on the other side of the market to keep the system solvent.

Crypto perps trade on two main types of venue.

Centralized exchanges, such as Binance, Bybit and OKX, run their own order books and hold owners' funds. They account for the vast majority of perps trading: Binance alone held about a third of centralized perps volume in early 2026, according to CoinGecko. Many are unavailable to U.S. customers.

It has been revealed that decentralized exchanges let traders use perps through smart contracts, while keeping control of their funds. Some, such as Hyperliquid and Solana-based Phoenix, run order books onchain, matching buyers and sellers much like a traditional exchange. Others, such as GMX and Jupiter, let traders trade against a shared pool of liquidity provided by other users.

Decentralized perps are growing fast. Their trading volume jumped from $1.5 trillion in 2024 to $6.38 trillion in 2025, led by Hyperliquid, CoinGecko found. Decentralized exchanges' share of perps trading volume peaked at 13% in late 2025 before slipping to 10% in April 2026, while their share of open interest, the total value of open positions, reached 13.5%.

In a recent development, in the U.S., perps developed largely on offshore exchanges, outside the reach of the CFTC, but that has started to change. In July 2025, Coinbase introduced CFTC-regulated "perpetual-style" futures for U.S. customers, with five-year expiries and up to 10x leverage. Two months later, CFTC-regulated exchange Bitnomial released what it called the first U.S. perpetual futures, with 25-year terms and eight-hour funding. In May 2026, the CFTC approved a Bitcoin perpetual futures contract from prediction market Kalshi and set out a framework for listing more, and in June, Kraken rolled out perps to eligible U.S. customers through Bitnomial, which its parent company had acquired.

Some of these contracts, including Kalshi's and Bitnomial's original design, have long but fixed terms of 25 years, so are not strictly perpetual. The regulator claims perps can be offered on CFTC-registered exchanges under federal oversight, and has advised U.S. traders to avoid offshore venues.

The shift has been contested. CME Group, the largest U.S. futures exchange, has sued the CFTC, arguing that perps are swaps rather than futures under U.S. law. The CFTC has nonetheless continued to approve more perps platforms, starting with Backpack.

In a recent development, perps are now spreading beyond crypto. Exchanges have begun listing perps tracking stocks, stock indexes, commodities such as gold and oil, and currencies, giving traders around-the-clock exposure to markets that normally close in the evening and on weekends.

Industry observers note that those products carry the same mechanics, and the same risks, as crypto perps. They track an asset's price without giving traders ownership of the asset itself, so a perp on a company's stock doesn't come with voting rights or dividends.

Perps can be useful tools for hedging and speculation, but they are among the riskiest products in crypto:.

Industry observers note that decrypt people can now trade perps directly alongside the news, through the Decrypt Money Account. The service is powered by Phoenix, a decentralized exchange on Solana, and lets users go long or short on crypto, stocks and commodities.

Availability varies by region, and as with any leveraged product, traders should only risk money they can afford to lose.

Decrypt offers perpetual futures trading through the Decrypt Money Account, powered by Phoenix.

It has been revealed that perpetual futures are leveraged products and carry a high risk of loss. Availability may vary by region. Nothing in this guide is investment advice.

Industry observers note that A sprawling living room might be the dream, but having a small space doesn’t preclude you from being able to stretch out on the couch. Sectionals specifically designed for smaller rooms prove that cozy movie nights and afternoon naps aren’t reserved exclusively for those with a massive floor blueprint. In fact, choosing a sectional with the right proportions stands to make a smaller room feel larger. There’s no reason to settle for a hodgepodge of chairs and ottomans when a thoughtfully selected sectional can transform every seat into the best seat in the house.

Being mindful of a space’s dimensions is always important when shopping for furniture, but especially so with a small room, where every inch may matter. Still, a variety of clever configurations—including L-shaped sectionals designed to nestle into corners, modular designs that are easily rearranged, and sofas with reversible chaises that give you more flexibility—cater to seemingly every layout. Add in performance fabrics, washable slipcovers, and supportive cushions, and you’ve got a recipe for some seriously comfortable yet compact lounging. Ahead, we’re sharing our favorite sectionals for small spaces that ensure every square foot counts.

According to recent reports, the best-selling Abisko sectional from Article is made even more beautiful by colorful, performance velvet upholstery. Suitable for those with little ones and pets running around, the fabric is non-absorptive, meaning spills and crumbs won’t stay embedded in its weave. Two orientations—chaise and L-shaped—allow you to Tetris its silhouette into your space as you see fit.

Sources indicate that instead of opting for a giant L-shaped sectional that will take up the entire room, aim for something with a smaller footprint. Available in performance fabric and three leg finishes, this sectional couch is ideal for a tiny living space and a major upgrade from a smaller loveseat thanks to the chaise addition. While not an official fold-out sleeper sofa, the back cushions flop back to give you enough space should you be inclined to nap. Contributor David Kaufman, who tested it out for us, calls it “a great starter sofa for a first home or apartment that you won’t have to send to a landfill when you’re ready to move.”.

Similar to the Thuma sectional contributor Evan Russum told us “feels solid and durable,” the Essential Sofa follows the brand’s signature simple-but-considered aesthetic with a minimalist silhouette,rounded cushions, and a grounded wooden base. Raised armrests add sculptural presence without overwhelming a small living room, while the detachable ottoman lets you switch between a left- or right-facing chaise—so everyone can have a turn on their favorite side of the sofa.

In a recent development, not your average grey couch, AllModern’s Jossa sectional is minimalist in looks but generous on comfort, thanks to its dense foam padding that offers plenty of support without feeling stiff. Easy to de-assemble, the modular design allows the sofa to evolve with your seating needs. Craving two separate lounge chairs? Done. Prefer a love seat? Just slide the two larger seats side-by-side. Today’s layout doesn’t have to be tomorrow’s.

The slim arms and low profile on this this reversible three-piece sectional make the Unwind especially suitable for a limited living area as it doesn’t monopolize the space. Five neutral color variations all come in a linen blend, but olive’s grounding tones are speaking most to us. This sectional, like many of the others on this list, can be configured to be left-facing or right-facing depending on your living room setup, and we particularly like that in case you tend to switch up your design layout (we certainly do).

At just 62 inches wide, Sabai’s Essential Loveseat Sectional demonstrates how even the smallest living rooms can accommodate a proper chaise lounge. The compact design features clean lines, a generously sized chaise, and supportive foam cushions, offering the ideal spot to stretch out after a long day. Adding to the sectional’s appeal is its focus on sustainability. It combines a frame made from wood certified by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC)—a third-party verification that ensures ethical wood sourcing—with upholstery fashioned from recycled natural materials. It’s also easy to clean and maintain, largely thanks to its washable slipcovers, sold separately—a welcome feature for anyone whose couch often doubles as a dining chair for meals eaten over the coffee table. Suffice it to say, this sectional is particularly well-suited to apartment living.

According to recent reports, CB2’s Deseo sectional brings a little drama to small-space living, courtesy of rich, praline-brown performance velvet, broad arms, and a low-slung silhouette that practically begs you to sink in and stay awhile. The three-piece configuration, matching ottoman, and option for an extra-deep seat only extend the lounging possibilities and allow you to take advantage of every inch of your space. If brown doesn’t fit your space’s palette, worry not; the Deseo comes in plenty of other glamorous colors, including seven other performance velvet upholstery options.

Recent findings suggest that serious lounging is the goal for Sundays’ Movie Night sectional, with oversized cushions, deep seats, and a relaxed silhouette that makes it difficult to resist the urge to spend the afternoon totally horizontal. The cream linen upholstery adds to its laid-back feel, while the movable ottoman lets you stretch out or create a more open seating arrangement when tech giant comes over. The company’s own LiveLife performance fabric is stain-resistant, moisture-repellent, and washable, with removable slipcovers that make living with a light-colored sofa significantly less intimidating.

Sources indicate that interior Define takes customization very seriously, and the Sloan sectional showcases how having such options can pay off in a small living room. Choose your preferred upholstery, cushion fill, seat depth, and leg style, then fine-tune the dimensions to suit your floor plan. The reversible chaise adds another layer of flexibility, allowing you to change its orientation, in case you rearrange your furniture or move to a new place with a different layout.

According to recent reports, contributor Malia Griggs tested the Sloan in her own 196-square-foot living room, where she found that its supportive cushions, tailored silhouette, and carefully selected dimensions worked beautifully alongside a narrow entryway. “If you enjoy tailoring your décor to your taste, are willing to pay a bit more for quality, and have the patience for a made-to-order process, this is a wonderful sectional—especially for a smaller space,” she added.

What Features Should I Look for in a Sectional for Small Living Rooms?

Sources indicate that modular furniture—any sectional that comes in several parts so you can adjust your sofa to suit the configurations—is built with flexibility in mind, making it the ideal contender for a small living space. We have tested and loved Castlery modular sofas, but a search for modular sectional should give you plenty of other options. A room tight on space can benefit from couches with storage, like those from Albany Park. Now you’ll be able to minimize the clutter and extra blankets by stowing them underneath your seat.

How Do I Arrange a Sectional in a Small Space?

Don’t fall for the tiniest sectional you can find, but rather invest in something well-made—it plays a big part in your living room, after all. While it may seem counterintuitive, Nashville interior designer Amanda Khouri indicates, “Filling a small room with small furniture can make it feel…well, smaller.”.

Designer Alicia Murphy used a sectional in the living room of a teensy trailer she converted into a plush family getaway in Montauk, Fresh York, for this very reason: “If you use a corner sectional rather than a sofa and chair, you most likely will add seating for two or three more people,” Murphy explains, noting that the alternative prevents you from having about 36 inches of dead space in the corner.”.

Another way to make it work? Set an L-shaped sectional across from two club chairs to create a conversation zone, advises interior designer Suzanne Dawson.

What Do I Look for in a High-Quality Sectional?

Recent findings suggest that when you’re working with a small space, quality counts. It’s much harder to get away with a mid-century modern knock-off when it’s one of four furniture pieces packed into the room. When shopping for a sectional, evaluate the materials and care instructions. Avoid anything with plywood, and polyester when you can. Seek out solid wood construction, such as walnut, oak, or teak; and premium fabrics, like linen, leather, or chenille. You’ll also want to keep the warranty and return policy in mind, in case you want to send back a piece that doesn’t work for you.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, THE STRUCTURE OF your workout over the course of weeks and months should depend on more than just the latest fitness fad. When you’re working toward a goal—whether that’s tied to building muscle, forging strength, losing weight, or improving performance—you’ll have the most success if you follow a blueprint. That plan (often called a workout split) should take into account arange of factors, including your specific goals, your experience level, schedule, and available equipment.

And one of the most well-known (and easy-to-understand) approaches to this is the Upper-Lower split, which is one of several workout splits organized around training different parts of the body on different days.

According to recent reports, an Upper-Lower Split program is broken down exactly as its name implies. One day you’ll train the muscle groups in your upper body (think chest, shoulders, back, arms); then the next you’ll train your lower body muscles (quads, glutes, hamstrings, calves). In general, that means your upper body gets to recover on days you’re training your lower body, and vice versa.

Recent findings suggest that this approach is one of a handful of training splits that works very well if you’re trying to add muscle, or if you’re somebody who’s chasing body recomposition. If you’re trying to build muscle, the more frequently you can train a muscle group with effective, hard sets, the better.

In a recent development, and an upper-lower split lets you train each muscle group at least twice a week, with solid rest in between each session. You’re training each muscle group more frequently than you would if you were doing a bro split (training just one body part a day). And you’re able to do more sets and exercises for key muscle groups than you would if you were doing a full-body training split.

Let’s break down the details of the upper-lower of split, along with a sample session you can use to put it into practice.

Sets and reps: 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps.

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps.

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 to 10 steps per leg.

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps per leg.

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 reps.

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 reps.

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps.

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps.

IF YOU WANT to understand the logic behind the workout above, here’s what you need to know. You'll alternate focusing on the upper body muscles and the lower body muscles in this split. Since you're no longer training the entire body, you'll have the time and energy to include a few more accessory motions. Over the course of the week, aim to hit all of the following movement patterns.

There are multiple ways to build an upper-lower split depending on your goals. But in general, think about including three to five exercises in every session.

YOU’RE ABLE TO hit major muscle groups more completely by splitting the body in half. Since we're able to add in a few accessory motions, we can start training in several different planes of motion, too. This split is well suited for recovery, since your upper body rests while you're working the lower body, and vice versa. That allows you to increase your frequency of training.

Industry observers note that YOU’RE STILL WORKING quite a few major muscle groups in a single workout, which can be fatiguing for the accessory movements added onto the end. If you’re in the awkward schedule space between having three and four days you can train, you might struggle to hit the upper/lower/upper/lower cadence that will be most effective—so stick to the more flexible full-body split.

Sources indicate that brett Williams, NASM-CPT, PES, a senior editor at Men's Health, is a certified trainer and former pro football player and tech reporter. You can find his work elsewhere at Mashable, Thrillist, and other outlets.

So, if you're a shower shaver, make sure to grab something waterproof and cordless.

According to recent reports, you also want to make sure your razor head can contour to your body's curves, especially when you're targeting areas like the bikini line, underarms, toes, and even legs. Some of the razors on this list, like the Panasonic Close Curves Electric Razor, can uniquely adapt to the body's curves with their rotating heads.

It has been revealed that if a razor is rechargeable (major plus already), make sure to check how long it takes to charge and the battery life. If you don't want to deal with a cord or annoying charge time, some of the options on this list—hi, Philips Series 5000 Electric Facial Hair Remover—are battery-powered, which may be more convenient while traveling.

Some razors come with trimmers, blade guides, and changeable blade heads for different areas of the body. If you're looking for more of a Swiss Army knife-type, multi-tool situation, take a look at the available attachments. Then, see if those are compatible with the parts of your body you want to tackle.

Believe it or not, many razors have a warranty, so if you're unsatisfied with your purchase, you can most likely return it for a longer period than you might think. Most razors on this list have a 30-day warranty, which gives you ample time for testing.

Our team tests a wide range of products and services to provide our readers with reliable, honest, and trustworthy information. It's our belief that our readers deserve the best, which is why our recommendations have been thoroughly tested and vetted by our very own editors. For the past year, Women’s Health editors, including myself, and contributors Jasmine Gomez and Sabrina Talbert, tested the bestselling, most popular, and top-rated electric razors. Our team also consulted four dermatologists, and then evaluated thousands of customer reviews and ratings to narrow down the seven best electric razors for a wide range of needs and preferences.

Recent findings suggest that ready for smooth, bump-free skin? Look no further than these editor-tested and expert-approved electric razors for women, below.

If you struggle with bumps and irritation, an electric razor might be your new best friend. Of course, you still need to make sure you use that electric razor properly. Dermatologists say you should follow the below best practices for a smooth shave every time.

Make sure your skin is well hydrated before shaving because using an electric razor over dry, irritated skin can make matters worse, says dermatologist Joshua Zeichner, MD. Dr. Robinson adds that you should also use a gentle cleanser prior to shaving. And, avoid fragrance or products known to cause irritation immediately before and after shaving, she says.

According to recent reports, and please, do so in the direction of the hair growth, claims Dr. Zeichner. Repeated strokes over the same area increase the likelihood of irritation and ingrown hairs.

Hydration is key. "I advise patients that they do not need a dedicated post-shave or aftercare lotion—a gentle moisturizer is just fine in these areas," indicates Dr. Robinson, who likes light, fragrance-free formulas. Aside from that, Dr. Robinson recommends making sure you follow any specific instructions on the product package—in other words, you should actually read the directions.

At the end of the day, everyone's going to have their personal preference, and it's not worth, ahem, splitting hairs if you prefer one type of razor over another. That being said, if your skin is prone to irritation, it might be time to ditch the traditional razor. With an electric razor, you’re not scraping against the skin really hard like a traditional razor does, indicates dermatologist Cameron Rokhsar, MD. This means that you won't see a lot of the cuts and burns that sometimes result from a manual blade, says Dr. Rokhsar. There are also areas of the body that might be better suited to shave with an electric razor. "Most women's electric razors are designed for our curvy areas," says Dr. Ploch. "I prefer electric razors around the ankles because manual razors cut this area easily.".

Keeping your electric razor clean is incredibly important, states Dr. Rokhsar. Many derms will recommend changing a manual razor every time you shave, but you can't do that with an electric one, which makes running the blades under warm water after use a crucial step. This will keep it free of hair, shaving cream, and other residues.

Dr. Rokhsar also recommends swiping over the blades and the outside of the razor with a rubbing alcohol-soaked cotton ball regularly. "Especially if it sits in your bathroom moisture, bacteria will accumulate on the blades," he says. "It's an easy entry point for bacteria to go down the hair follicle." That's a substantial no-no if you want to stay free of irritation or infection.

Our team of editors follow Dr. Rokhsar's advice and it hasn't led us astray. And despite evaluating some of these razors for close to a year, we are pleased that we haven't noticed any rusting after using the alcohol-soaked cotton ball.

In a recent development, another tip is to actually read and follow the maintenance instructions of your device. (Admittedly, we threw ours away since we've been using these for several months and like to keep the limited space of our beauty closet as streamlined as possible.) You can also prioritize using devices like the Philips Series 5000 Electric Facial Hair Remover that's easy to clean, as the head can easily be removed so you can dump shaved hair and dead skin cells straight into the garbage.

According to recent reports, scottish football manager Steve Evans is “feeling the best I've felt in years and years” after 90 pounds in just six months. After Rotherham dropped him in March last year, Evans decided to focus on improving his health before jumping straight back in at another club.

Industry observers note that and it's worked wonders for the 64-year-old, who has meticulously stuck to the plan prescribed to him by health specialists and trainers. It hasn't been easy for Evans, but he's managed to improve his diet and increase his activity levels to a point where he now swims 2.5km every morning, cycles regularly and gets in plenty of steps by walking his dogs daily.

“Here we are six months or so later, six and a half stone down,” he told Sky Sports. “It has been incredibly hard work, but I am feeling the benefit now mentally and physically, feeling fantastic.”.

Sources indicate that after waking up and taking his dogs on a walk first thing in the morning, Evans then grabs his swimming trunks and heads to the pool at his local gym. While there, he'll swim at least 2.5km, though sometimes further if he's feeling good in the water. Evans also cycles on the exercise bike at the gym to supplement his training, as well as spending some time sitting in the sauna.

In total, Evans spends around two-and-a-half hours in the gym, while he ensures he keeps his diet healthy with lots of protein and a reduced calorie intake. And, if he still has some energy left at the end of the day, the 64-year-old will take his dogs out on another walk in the evening to add a few more steps to his daily total.

Recent findings suggest that evans couldn't just jump straight into that level of activity, however. He needed to take gradual steps to build up to the 2.5km he now swims everyday, after recognizing that he had started to neglect his health while working as a football manager.

According to recent reports, “I came out of Rotherham and within a few days made some family decisions,” he told Sky Sports. “I sat down with the family and, despite the phone ringing from a couple of clubs, I made the decision to get healthy and fitter. It's something I hadn't done for a lot of years. I went to see some serious people and some specialists, a cardiologist and fitness people. We came up with a initiative and my family did not think I would be able to do it.”.

In a recent development, “I was worried about myself,” he admitted. “My doctor at Royal Papworth gave me a plan. That plan was obviously a substantially reduced intake of calories and a gradual fitness program to then go and work with a fitness coach.”.

In a recent development, “It started off with swimming 10 lengths of a pool, which I found really tough at the time, and doing so many walks and so many jogs, to building up to now where I comfortably go and swim 70 to 80 lengths every morning. I had to make sure that I was mentally in tune with that—it's been brilliant and I'm feeling the best I've felt in years and years.”.

Recent findings suggest that having worked so hard to achieve such impressive results, Evans isn't intent on stopping any time soon. Indeed, he's targeting even more weight loss and will look to add some strength and conditioning work in the near future to further contribute to his lifestyle change.

“It's a little bit more weight loss for another two-to-three weeks, and then hopefully by that time it'll be about conditioning, which will be another tough part to go through, but I'm looking forward to the challenge,” he added. “My body internally is actually in really good shape now after all the scans I had last week.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD’s new EV may be about the size of a Toyota Camry, but it’s playing in a whole different league when it comes to technology.

BYD introduced the second-generation Seal 07 last week, calling it “the newly introduced choice for a class-leading luxury experience.”.

It’s available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with prices starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

Both versions measure 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly longer than the Toyota Camry.

Don’t let the price fool you, however, the vehicle is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough technology.

The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery that provides a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

Thanks to the second-gen Blade Batteries and BYD’s Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes.

The Seal 07 is also BYD’s first vehicle to debut with its new Disus-M Intelligent Magnetorheological Body Control System.

Industry observers note that the setup features a front double-wishbone suspension and an enhanced rear five-link suspension. It works alongside BYD’s road-surface sensors that use LiDAR, plus its iTAC 2.0 Intelligent Torque Adaptation System.

Zhang Zhuo, the general manager of BYD’s Ocean sales division, offered a better look at how the system works in real life in the video shown above.

Industry observers note that BYD stated the system provides ultra-fast response times down to the millisecond. The advanced suspension system adjusts damping force across a wide range of 100 to 10,000 Nm.

Recent findings suggest that it’s equipped on the all-electric Flagship Seal 07 variant, while lower-priced versions have the Disus-C intelligent body control system. The top-spec EV model with the Disus-M setup starts at 172,900 yuan ($26,000). Still, not too bad for what you get.

Inside, the new Seal 07 adopts BYD’s new interior design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens.

BYD added a few premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio.

Sources indicate that quite impressive for sure. What's more impressive is that GM/Cadillac first offered magnetic ride control back in 2002 (a full 24 years ago!!). It may not have been quite as advanced as this system in 2026, but still one of the most advanced suspension systems offered to date for a line of vehicles.

According to recent reports, I really want this car!! I truly hope BYD will be able to sell this in the USA soon.

The Seal 07 also debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that lets drivers interact with the vehicle and manage functions remotely.

Higher-priced versions are available with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, which includes a roof-mounted LiDAR. The setup provides safety and convenience features like Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super trade-in price” special, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the newly introduced Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.

Bonus: a hidden waistband pocket makes it easy to stash small essentials on the go. As a runner myself, I’ve found them perfect for carrying keys during jogs—they always stay in place.

Plus, the compression holds up through everything from weightlifting to yoga, and the high-waisted fit is both flattering and comfortable. According to recent reports, when we put them to the test at the gym, we really appreciated the moisture-wicking material. Even after a hot yoga class, I felt way drier than I was expecting.

According to recent reports, after testing this legging, we agree that their softness is top-notch. These leggings have the most inseam options on this list, ranging from 25 inches to 31 inches if you're on the taller side. In terms of sizing, our testers find that these leggings run totally true-to-size, which, if you're an avid Amazon shopper, you know is hard to come by.

Professor Preeti Arya, PhD, specializes in textile development at the Fashion Institute of Technology. She claims that the right fabric for leggings depends on your needs. But if you're worried about maintenance, "you can go for something that is petroleum-based because care is easy," she says. Petroleum-based fabrics include spandex, polyester, and nylon. These options are also typically much cheaper, according to Arya, but you can also opt for wool or silk, which sometimes feel better on your skin since they're natural fibers. Heads up: these fabrics are a bit harder to care for, though, and require special attention on laundry day.

It has been revealed that rise is really up to your personal preference, but higher-rise leggings usually have tummy control, which is a plus when you want to feel snatched at the gym. However, tummy control typically comes with a bit more compression, which may not be great for lower-impact activities like yoga or casual walks.

In a recent development, again, length is up to your personal preference, but the most flattering cut is typically just above your ankle. For most people, that means a 7/8 style of leggings. Full-length leggings, or ones that extend all the way to your feet, might be better for barefoot workouts like yoga. Other lengths, like capri leggings, are really up to your personal style.

Latest Update: Europe’s electric car sales jump 49% as global EV sales grow

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026.
  • Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
  • Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a big catch.

Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.

Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.

Recent findings suggest that europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.

Sources indicate that that puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.

Industry observers note that sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how quickly the market is growing.

Industry observers note that germany’s EV share topped 45% of fresh car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.

UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.

And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of latest car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.

Industry observers note that north American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.

US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.

But here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.

October 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.

“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” said Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.

The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.

China sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.

Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.

Even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s new car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.

Industry observers note that chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of upcoming energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.

Sources indicate that those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.

Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.

Australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.

It has been revealed that brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.

Nothing like consumer economics to drive sales. Local story about consumer economics: Windturbines on land is not popular. However, the locals realised they could heat their home for $300/year (in Denmark(!)) with these wind turbines and then they were tolerated! Same with cars - people gravitate to cheaper alternatives despite the more frequent charging and initial higher prices.

In a recent development, as the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.
